card.headline: Active fish rushing to feed
card.look: Healthy tilapia swim together in calm groups and rush to the surface when feed is thrown. Healthy catfish feed hard and fast. Colours are bright, fins are whole and the body is smooth with no spots or sores.
card.action: Watch your fish every day at feeding time and test the water regularly, so you notice any change from normal early.

detail.summary: This page describes what healthy Nile tilapia and African catfish (kambale) look like, and the pond water conditions they need to stay that way. Fish cannot tell you when they feel unwell, and many fish problems start with poor water rather than germs. If you know clearly what normal looks like in your pond, you will spot trouble days earlier. That gives you time to act before you lose fish, feed and money.
detail.cause: Fish health depends mostly on the water they live in. Unlike cattle or chickens, fish breathe, eat, drink and get rid of waste all in the same water. So water quality is the main thing that keeps them healthy. Fish need enough dissolved oxygen, which is oxygen mixed into the water that they take in through their gills. They also need a steady temperature, a pH (a measure of how acidic or alkaline the water is) in a safe range, and low ammonia. Ammonia is a poisonous waste that fish give off through their gills and that also comes from rotting leftover feed and manure. Useful general targets from FAO and Kenyan extension guidance are these. Water temperature should be about 25–30°C for both tilapia and catfish; below about 20°C they eat little and grow slowly. Dissolved oxygen should ideally stay above 5 mg/L; tilapia get stressed below about 3 mg/L. Catfish cope better with low oxygen because they can gulp air, but they still grow best in good water. pH should be about 6.5–8.5. Ammonia should be as close to zero as possible; the toxic form (un-ionised ammonia) should stay below about 0.05 mg/L. Ammonia becomes more poisonous when water is warm and pH is high. Pond water should be light green, from healthy algae (tiny water plants), so that a white disc or your palm disappears at roughly 30–40 cm depth. Next comes good nutrition. Fish need a balanced feed with the right protein for their size, fed in amounts they finish quickly. They need fair stocking density, meaning not too many fish for the pond size. Finally, stress must be kept low. Stress from rough handling, crowding, sudden water changes or poor water weakens the immune system and the protective slime on the skin. That lets bacteria, parasites and fungi take hold.
spread: Most fish health problems are triggered by poor water quality: low oxygen, high ammonia, sudden temperature changes or pH swings stress fish before any germ is involved.
Oxygen is lowest just before dawn, because algae use up oxygen at night. It is worst after several cloudy days, during very hot calm weather, or when a thick algal bloom suddenly dies.
Overfeeding is a common trigger. Uneaten feed rots at the bottom, uses up oxygen and releases ammonia.
New fingerlings from uncertified sources can bring parasites and bacteria into a clean pond.
Heavy rain can wash soil, manure, pesticides or wild fish into ponds, causing muddy water and pH changes. This is most common in the long rains (March to May) and short rains (October to December).
Rough netting, sorting and transport damage the protective slime and scales, opening the way for infection.
Birds, frogs, wild fish and shared nets or buckets can carry parasites and germs between ponds.
detail.atRisk: Fingerlings and newly stocked fish are the most fragile, especially in the first two weeks after transport. Crowded ponds and ponds that are fed heavily are at greater risk of oxygen crashes and ammonia build-up. Tilapia are more sensitive to low oxygen than catfish. Catfish in crowded tanks tend to bite each other and develop skin wounds. In the hot dry season (roughly January to March) warm, still water holds less oxygen and blooms can crash. During the rains, runoff and muddy water are bigger risks. In highland areas such as Nyeri, Kiambu and Meru, the cold season (June to August) brings water temperatures that slow feeding and weaken fish. Liner ponds and tanks without aeration, recirculating systems where a pump can fail, and ponds fertilised with too much manure need extra care.

early: Tilapia swim together in loose, calm groups at mid-depth and move away smoothly when your shadow falls over the pond.
Fish rush to the feed within seconds and eat it all within about 10–15 minutes, leaving little or nothing floating or sinking.
Tilapia have clear, bright colours with a shiny silver-grey to olive body. Breeding males may show darker or reddish colours on the head and fins, which is normal.
Catfish are smooth, dark grey-olive to mottled, with a clean slimy skin, long whole barbels (the 'whiskers') and strong, quick movements.
Fins are whole, held open and smooth-edged, with no frayed tips, red streaks or white cotton-like patches.
Gills are bright red to deep pink when you gently lift the gill cover of a netted fish, with no pale, brown, grey or swollen patches.
Eyes are clear and sit normally in the head, not cloudy, bulging or sunken.
Fish in a group are a fairly even size and grow steadily when you sample-weigh them every few weeks.
Pond water is light green, smells fresh or earthy, and there are no dead fish at the edges or the outlet.
advanced: Fish come slowly to feed, eat only part of it, or leave feed floating. This is often the very first sign that water or health is going wrong.
Many tilapia gulp at the surface in the early morning or crowd at the water inlet. This means low oxygen and needs action that same morning.
A fish swims alone, sits still at the edge or bottom, swims in circles or on its side, or flashes and rubs its body against the pond bottom or walls.
The skin turns dull, very dark or pale, has too much slime or too little, or shows red spots, sores, white or grey cotton-like patches or missing scales.
Fins become frayed, ragged, reddened at the base or eaten away, or are held clamped tightly against the body.
Gills look pale, brown, blotchy or swollen, or the gill covers stay flared and move fast.
Eyes become cloudy or bulging, or the belly becomes swollen.
The water suddenly changes colour (very dark green, brown, grey or clear after being green), smells bad, or a few fish are found dead each day.

lookalikes.name: Catfish coming up for air
lookalikes.howToTell: African catfish are air-breathers. They normally rise briefly to gulp air and dive straight back down, even in good water. Worry only if they hang at the surface for long periods, if they stop feeding, or if tilapia in the same pond are also gasping at the surface.

lookalikes.name: Tilapia breeding behaviour
lookalikes.howToTell: Mature male tilapia dig round nests in the pond bottom, darken in colour, chase other fish and may have small nips on the fins. Females may stop eating while they carry eggs or fry in their mouths. The fish are otherwise active and their skin is clean. Sick fish are dull, slow and often show sores or frayed fins on many fish, not just a few chasing ones.

lookalikes.name: Slow feeding in cold weather
lookalikes.howToTell: In the cold season, or on cold mornings in the highlands, all the fish eat less and move slowly because the water is cool. The water thermometer will read below about 22°C. Feeding picks up as the water warms in the afternoon, and there are no sores, gasping or deaths. In that case reduce feed rather than treating.

lookalikes.name: Stress after stocking or handling
lookalikes.howToTell: Fish that have just been transported, netted or sorted may hide, change colour and eat poorly for a few days. If water quality is good and they return to normal feeding within about a week with no wounds spreading, it was handling stress. If sores, fungus or deaths appear, call for advice.

detail.diagnosis: You cannot take a fish's temperature the way you do with a cow. Instead, a home fish health check means checking the water, then watching the fish, then looking closely at a few fish. Do it the same way every time so you can compare. First, the water. Use a pond thermometer at about 30 cm depth, morning and afternoon. Use a simple test kit, sold by agrovets, aquaculture suppliers and some county fisheries offices, to check pH and ammonia at least weekly, and more often in tanks or crowded ponds. If you can get a dissolved oxygen meter or kit, test at dawn, when oxygen is lowest. Check water colour and clarity with a white disc or your hand: if you lose sight of it at shallower than about 20 cm the bloom is too thick, and if you can see past about 60 cm the water is too clear and poor in natural food. Second, watch the fish at feeding time. Note how fast they come, how much they eat, and whether any fish stay away. Look at the pond edges and outlet every morning for dead or weak fish. Third, every few weeks, gently net a small sample of fish with wet hands or a soft net. Look at the skin, fins, eyes and gills, then weigh them and return them quickly, keeping them out of water for as short a time as possible. Write everything in a pond record book: date, water readings, feed given, feeding response, deaths and sample weights. If something looks wrong, a fisheries officer or fish vet will want this record. They may also ask you to bring live, sick fish in a container of pond water with air, because dead fish spoil quickly and are hard to test. They can then examine skin scrapings and gills under a microscope, or send samples to a laboratory such as KMFRI or a veterinary lab.
firstSteps: Watch your fish at every feeding and check the pond edges and outlet each morning, so you know clearly what normal looks like in your own pond.
Feed only what the fish clear in about 10–15 minutes, and reduce feed at once if they are slow to eat or the water is cold.
If fish gasp at the surface at dawn, stop feeding that day, add fresh well-oxygenated water or run an aerator, and splash or agitate the water if you have nothing else.
Test water temperature, pH and ammonia regularly, and immediately whenever the fish behave differently.
Remove dead or dying fish quickly and bury them away from the pond, because rotting fish foul the water and spread germs.
Keep separate nets and buckets for each pond, or clean and dry them in the sun between ponds.
Wash your hands after handling fish or pond water, and cover any cuts on your hands.
Write down feeding, water readings and any deaths, and call your County Fisheries Officer, an aquaculture extension officer or a vet early if changes do not settle within a day or two.
detail.vetTreatment: Healthy fish do not need routine medicines. Fish health care in Kenya is mostly about prevention and advice. It is provided by County Fisheries Officers, the Kenya Fisheries Service, KMFRI and other research stations, aquaculture extension officers, and vets trained in fish health. Useful routine support includes advice on pond design, stocking density, liming (adding agricultural lime to correct acid water) and fertilising. Officers can also help you test water, train you to sample and weigh fish, and check hatchery fingerlings. When fish do get sick, the officer or vet first looks for a water problem, because fixing the water often solves the problem without any drug. If a parasite, bacterium or fungus is confirmed, they may advise salt baths, improved water management, or in some cases a licensed medicine. Any medicine, especially antibiotics in feed or water, must only be used when prescribed by a vet. Treating a whole pond is costly, can harm the pond ecosystem, and careless use breeds antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. Any treated fish must not be harvested or sold until the withdrawal period stated by the vet has passed, so that no drug residues reach consumers.
prevention: Buy fingerlings only from hatcheries certified by the Kenya Fisheries Service. Check that they are active and even-sized, and acclimatise them by floating the bag in the pond for 15–30 minutes before slowly mixing in pond water.
Stock at the density recommended by your fisheries officer for your pond type and aeration. Crowding is one of the most common causes of poor water and disease.
Feed a good-quality feed with the right pellet size and protein for the fish's age. Store it dry and off the floor to stop mould, and never feed mouldy or caked feed.
Test water regularly, keep pH in range using agricultural lime on acidic soils as advised, and avoid over-fertilising with manure.
Keep oxygen up with aeration or fresh water flow where possible, especially in the hot season, in crowded ponds and after cloudy days.
Dig cut-off drains around ponds so rainwater runoff, soil and chemicals do not wash in. Screen inlets to keep out wild fish.
Handle fish gently and as little as possible, using wet hands and soft nets. Sort or harvest in the cool early morning.
Dry and lime ponds between production cycles where practical. Keep grass trimmed around the banks and discourage predatory birds.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan fish farm, feed is usually the biggest cost. Healthy fish turn that feed into growth efficiently. They reach market size on time and fetch better prices from hotels, fish traders and local markets that want even-sized, fresh-looking fish. When water or health goes wrong, the first loss is often invisible. Fish eat less, grow slowly, and wasted feed rots in the pond, so you pay for feed that never becomes fish. Next come scattered deaths, then sometimes sudden mass deaths after an oxygen crash, which can wipe out a pond overnight. Poor-looking fish with sores or uneven sizes sell for less, and buyers may lose trust. Daily observation and regular water testing cost little compared with losing a whole crop.
detail.humanHealth: Healthy, well-handled fish pose little risk to people, but basic hygiene still matters. A few germs found in pond water and fish, such as certain Streptococcus and Mycobacterium bacteria, can infect cuts on the hands of people who handle fish. Wear gloves or cover cuts, avoid spines puncturing the skin, and wash hands with soap after handling fish or pond water. Cook fish thoroughly. If fish have ever been treated with any medicine, follow the vet's withdrawal period strictly before eating or selling them, to avoid drug residues in food.
detail.outlook: Fish kept in good water, fed correctly and stocked at the right density usually stay healthy and grow well through the cycle. Most early warning signs come from water quality, such as slow feeding, morning gasping or dull colours. When they are caught within a day or two and the water is corrected, fish often recover fully without medicine. Recovery is less likely when problems are noticed late, when many fish already have sores or gill damage, or when the cause, such as overcrowding, overfeeding or no aeration, is not fixed. Keeping records and knowing your normal baseline is the best protection.

faqs.q: Why do my fish come to the surface early in the morning?
faqs.a: If catfish rise briefly to gulp air and dive again, that is normal because they are air-breathers. If tilapia, or many fish of either kind, hang at the surface gasping at dawn, oxygen is too low. Stop feeding that day and add fresh water or aeration. Then look for the cause: overfeeding, too many fish, a thick algal bloom, or several cloudy days. Test the water and talk to your fisheries officer if it happens again.

faqs.q: What colour should my pond water be?
faqs.a: A light to medium green is best. It shows healthy algae that produce oxygen and natural food. If you can still see your hand or a white disc deeper than about 60 cm, the water is too clear and may need fertilising as advised. If it disappears above about 20 cm, or the water is very dark green, brown or smells bad, the bloom is too thick or dying. Reduce feed and fertiliser and add fresh water.

faqs.q: How do I know I am feeding the right amount?
faqs.a: Watch the fish. The right amount is what they eat eagerly and finish in about 10–15 minutes. If feed is left floating or sinking, you are overfeeding, which wastes money and fouls the water. Feed needs change as fish grow and as water temperature changes, so sample-weigh fish every few weeks. Ask your extension officer or feed supplier for a feeding guide matched to fish size.

faqs.q: Should I add antibiotics to the feed to prevent disease?
faqs.a: No. Healthy fish do not need antibiotics. Adding them 'just in case' wastes money and leaves residues in fish meant for people. It also breeds germs that no longer respond to medicine. Prevention comes from clean water, good feed, correct stocking and careful handling. Medicines should only be used when a vet has confirmed a bacterial disease and prescribed them, and you must observe the withdrawal period before selling fish.

faqs.q: Can I keep tilapia and catfish in the same pond?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Kenyan farmers keep them together, and catfish help by eating the extra tilapia fry that cause overcrowding. Stock the catfish at the right ratio and size so they do not eat your main tilapia crop. Remember that the pond now carries more fish, so watch oxygen and feeding closely. Your fisheries officer can advise on ratios for your pond.

faqs.q: How often should I test my pond water?
faqs.a: Check temperature daily if you can, and pH and ammonia at least once a week in earth ponds. Test more often in tanks, liner ponds, crowded ponds and recirculating systems. Always test straight away if fish stop feeding, gasp, or change behaviour. Testing oxygen at dawn tells you the worst point of the day. Write all results down so you can see trends.

healthy.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a school of healthy Nile tilapia with bright silver-olive scales and fully intact fins rushing to floating feed pellets at the surface of a light-green earthen fish pond in rural Kenya on a sunny morning.
healthy.seoDescription: How to tell healthy tilapia and catfish: active schooling, strong feeding, bright colour, red gills, and pond targets for oxygen, pH and ammonia.

card.headline: Fish gasping at the water surface
card.look: At dawn, many fish crowd at the surface with their mouths open, gulping air, or pack together where fresh water flows in. They ignore feed, and big fish may suddenly be found dead along the edges.
card.action: Stop feeding at once and get fresh, splashing, oxygen-rich water or aeration into the pond immediately.

detail.summary: Low oxygen happens when the water does not hold enough dissolved oxygen (oxygen mixed invisibly into the water, which fish breathe through their gills). It is one of the most common causes of sudden mass fish deaths in Kenyan tilapia and catfish ponds. It can kill a whole pond in one night, often just before sunrise. It is an emergency, but it can usually be prevented with good feeding, stocking and water management.
detail.cause: Fish take oxygen from the water through their gills, so the water must keep enough of it. In a fish pond, most oxygen comes from tiny green plants called algae (the green colour in the water) or phytoplankton. They make oxygen in sunlight. At night, and on dull cloudy days, the algae stop making oxygen but keep using it, along with the fish and the bacteria breaking down waste. So oxygen falls all night and is lowest just before dawn. Problems arise when this night-time demand is too high. Common reasons are too many fish, too much feed or manure, a very thick algae bloom, or several cloudy days in a row. Uneaten feed, fish droppings and manure rot on the pond bottom, and the bacteria doing the rotting use up large amounts of oxygen. A sudden algae die-off, also called a crash, is especially dangerous. Millions of algae die at once, stop producing oxygen, and their rotting bodies use up even more. Warm water holds less oxygen than cool water, while warm fish need more. Heavy cold rain or strong wind can also suddenly mix oxygen-poor bottom water into the whole pond, which is called a pond turnover. When oxygen drops, fish first move to the surface to gulp the thin oxygen-rich top layer. If levels keep falling, their gills cannot supply the body, they become weak, lose balance and die of suffocation. Larger fish need more oxygen and usually die first.
spread: Low oxygen is not an infection and does not spread from fish to fish, but it can hit every fish in the pond at the same time.
Several cloudy, rainy or still days in a row reduce sunlight, so algae produce less oxygen while demand stays high.
Overfeeding leaves uneaten pellets on the pond bottom, where they rot and use up oxygen, especially overnight.
Overstocking means too many fish breathing the same water. Problems often appear as fish grow bigger towards harvest.
Too much manure, chicken droppings or fertiliser causes a very thick algae bloom that can suddenly crash and die.
Hot weather, very warm water, or water flow stopping (a dry inlet, broken pump, power cut, or blocked canal) can quickly tip a borderline pond into crisis.
Heavy cold rain, strong winds or disturbing deep, smelly bottom mud can mix oxygen-poor water and harmful gases such as hydrogen sulphide (rotten-egg smell) through the pond.
Using pesticides or herbicides near the pond, or chemicals that kill algae, can cause an algae die-off followed by an oxygen crash.
detail.atRisk: All farmed fish can suffocate. Tilapia, the most common pond fish in Kenya, cope with fairly low oxygen for short periods, but they still die when levels crash. African catfish (Clarias, locally called mumi or kamongo) can breathe some air from the surface, so they often survive when tilapia die. However, crowded catfish can still suffer, especially if they cannot reach the surface. Large fish close to harvest are most at risk because they need the most oxygen and the pond carries its heaviest load then. Fry and fingerlings in small tanks, hapas or transport bags are also very vulnerable. High-risk systems include intensively fed earthen ponds and liner ponds with little or no water exchange, backyard ponds fertilised heavily with manure, and recirculating or tank systems that depend on pumps and electricity. The highest-risk times are the long and short rains, when skies stay cloudy for days, hot still periods, and the hours between about midnight and sunrise. Ponds in warm lowland areas such as parts of Western, Nyanza and Coast regions, and ponds that have not been drained and desilted for several cycles, face extra risk.

early: Fish come to the surface early in the morning and gulp air with their mouths, a behaviour called piping. Small ripples or popping sounds may be heard across the pond.
Fish crowd together near the water inlet, a waterfall or wherever fresh water enters, and stay there.
Fish refuse feed or eat much less than usual, especially at the morning feed.
Fish swim slowly and sluggishly near the surface or edges instead of staying deeper in the pond.
The water colour changes suddenly, for example from bright green to brown, grey, milky or unusually clear. This is a sign the algae may be dying.
The pond may smell stale, earthy or like rotten eggs, and foam or scum may appear on the surface.
Gill covers move fast and wide as fish breathe harder, and gills may look pale when a fish is examined.
advanced: Large numbers of fish stay at the surface gasping even after sunrise, and they do not dive away when you approach or clap.
Fish lose balance, swim on their sides or in circles, or lie weak at the pond edges.
Sudden deaths occur, often overnight or at dawn, with the biggest fish dying first and many found floating or along the banks.
Dead fish may have mouths wide open and gill covers flared out.
Catfish may still be gulping while most tilapia are dead, or even catfish start dying in severe cases.
Within hours, a whole pond can be lost if oxygen is not restored.

lookalikes.name: Ammonia or nitrite poisoning (brown blood disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: These also cause gasping because the toxic waste stops blood carrying oxygen. They often follow heavy feeding in ponds or tanks with poor water exchange. With nitrite, the gills and blood may look chocolate-brown instead of bright red. Gasping may continue during the day even when oxygen is good. A water test kit for ammonia and nitrite tells them apart.

lookalikes.name: Gill parasites or bacterial gill disease (e.g. columnaris)
lookalikes.howToTell: Damaged gills cause fish to gasp and crowd at the inlet, but deaths usually build up over several days rather than all at once overnight. Fish of all sizes may be affected, and you may see swollen, slimy, patchy or rotting gills, white or yellow patches on the body, or flashing (rubbing against the bottom). Fish keep gasping even when oxygen levels are good. Diagnosis needs a fisheries or vet lab check of gill samples.

lookalikes.name: Chemical or pesticide poisoning
lookalikes.howToTell: Deaths are sudden and may follow spraying of nearby crops, runoff after rain, or cattle dip washings entering the water. Fish may twitch, jump, or swim wildly in spirals rather than just gasping quietly. Small fish, frogs and insects in the pond may die too. Oxygen levels may be normal at first. Note the timing and any nearby spraying.

lookalikes.name: Heat stress from very warm water
lookalikes.howToTell: Shallow ponds and tanks overheat on hot sunny afternoons, and fish become stressed and gasp in the heat of the day, not mainly at dawn. Warm water also holds less oxygen, so the two problems often overlap. A thermometer reading and the time of day help separate them.

detail.diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly made by measuring dissolved oxygen and reading the signs and timing. A County Fisheries Officer, Kenya Fisheries Service officer, aquaculture extension officer or fish vet will usually test the water with a dissolved oxygen meter or chemical test kit. Testing at or just before dawn gives the most useful reading, because oxygen is lowest then. As a general guide, warm-water pond fish do best when oxygen is kept well above about 5 milligrams per litre and become stressed when it falls much below about 3. Fish start dying when it stays very low, although tolerance differs between species and sizes. The officer will also check water temperature, pH (acidity), ammonia and nitrite, and look at the water colour, depth of visibility and bottom condition. If fish are still dying after oxygen is restored, they may examine gills and send fresh or chilled fish to a lab, such as KMFRI or a veterinary laboratory, to rule out parasites, bacteria or poisoning. To help, the farmer should note when gasping and deaths started, and how many and what size fish died. Record recent weather (cloudy days, heavy rain), feeding amounts, stocking numbers, any manure or fertiliser added, changes in water colour or smell, and any spraying nearby. Keep two or three freshly dead or dying fish cool, not frozen, in a clean bag for examination.
firstSteps: Stop feeding immediately and do not feed again until fish are behaving normally. Uneaten and digesting feed uses up oxygen the fish need to survive.

Add fresh, clean, oxygen-rich water straight away, ideally from a stream, borehole or canal. Let it fall or splash onto the surface so it picks up air. At the same time, let out bottom water from the drain if your pond allows it.

Create aeration (mixing air into water). Run a paddlewheel or aerator if you have one, or use a pump to spray water back onto the pond surface. In an emergency, people can splash and stir the surface with paddles, boards or buckets, working in shifts.
Do not stir up or disturb the bottom mud, and do not drain the pond very low. Bottom mud is oxygen-poor and can release harmful gases.
Do not add manure, fertiliser, lime, salt or any chemical as an emergency fix, as these do not add oxygen and some make things worse.

Remove dead and dying fish quickly using a net and gloves. Bury them away from the water with lime or soil, or dispose of them as your officer advises, because rotting fish use oxygen and attract predators.
Keep safe. Keep electric pumps and cables well away from water and people, never work alone at a deep pond at night, and keep children away from the edges.

Call your County Fisheries Officer or aquaculture extension officer, and record times, numbers and sizes of dead fish, weather and feeding. Keep checking the pond through the night and the next dawn, because oxygen may fall again.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that cures low oxygen. The treatment is to restore oxygen and remove its causes. A fisheries officer or fish vet will usually confirm oxygen levels with a meter, then advise on emergency aeration, water exchange and how long to withhold feed. Next, they will help you find the root cause, such as overstocking, overfeeding, too much manure, an algae crash, or a failed water supply. They may recommend partial harvest to reduce the number of fish, adjusting feed amounts, or changing how you fertilise. Where a turnover or rotten bottom is suspected, they may advise draining, drying and desilting the pond after harvest. Survivors are stressed and may develop infections in the following days and weeks. If disease appears, the officer may take samples and, only if a bacterial infection is confirmed, a vet may prescribe a treatment such as a medicated feed. Antibiotics do nothing for low oxygen itself, and using them without a diagnosis wastes money and encourages antimicrobial resistance (germs no longer responding to medicines). Any medicine must be prescribed by a vet and comes with a withdrawal period, a waiting time before fish can be harvested and eaten, which must be followed strictly. Expect fish to resume feeding within a day or two if the crisis was caught early. Restart feeding with small amounts.
prevention: Stock at a density suited to your pond, water supply and aeration. Follow guidance from your fisheries officer or KALRO/KMFRI materials rather than adding extra fish, because problems often appear as fish grow.
Feed carefully. Give only what fish eat within a short time, watch that feed is cleared, and adjust amounts as fish grow. Never dump extra feed to speed up growth.
Reduce or skip feeding on cloudy, rainy or very hot still days, and whenever fish show any surface gasping in the morning.

Go to the pond at dawn every day and look for fish at the surface. This simple habit catches most problems before mass deaths. If you can, get a dissolved oxygen meter or test kit, or ask your extension officer to test regularly.

Manage the green water. Use manure and fertiliser only in moderate amounts as advised. A simple check is to put your arm in the water: if the water is so thick you cannot see your hand just below the surface, the bloom is too dense. Stop fertilising and add fresh water.
Keep a reliable supply of fresh water and a way to aerate. Consider an aerator, paddlewheel or spray pump for intensive ponds, along with a backup plan for power cuts or a dry inlet.

Between production cycles, drain, dry and remove excess black mud from the pond bottom. Keep ponds at a sensible depth, and cut back overgrown water weeds and overhanging vegetation that rot in the water.
Harvest or partly harvest fish once they reach market size rather than holding very heavy fish in the pond. Keep pesticide spraying, dip wash and runoff away from ponds.
detail.impact: Low oxygen is one of the fastest ways a Kenyan fish farmer can lose an investment. A single bad night can kill most of the fish in a pond, and the biggest fish, which have eaten the most feed and are closest to sale, usually die first. The farmer loses the cost of fingerlings and months of feed, and often the expected harvest income or school fees. Fish that die in the pond quickly spoil in warm weather and usually cannot be sold. Repeated mild low-oxygen periods that do not kill fish still cause poor appetite, slow growth, poor feed conversion (more feed for each kilo of fish) and weaker immunity, so disease outbreaks become more likely. For groups and commercial farms supplying hotels, schools or markets, sudden losses can also break supply contracts and damage trust. Prevention through careful feeding, sensible stocking and simple aeration costs far less than a single crash.
detail.humanHealth: Low oxygen itself does not infect people. However, fish that are found dead in the pond, especially after some hours in warm water, spoil quickly and can cause food poisoning. They should not be sold or eaten unless they were collected while still alive and fresh and handled hygienically, and if unsure, dispose of them safely. Wear gloves when handling dead fish and wash hands well afterwards. Take care with electric pumps near water and with deep ponds at night, as drowning and electric shock are real risks during emergencies.
detail.outlook: If the problem is noticed early, at the first signs of gasping, and oxygen is restored quickly with fresh water and aeration, most fish usually survive. They start feeding again within a day or two. Once mass deaths have started, losses can be heavy, and the outcome depends on how quickly oxygen is raised and how big and crowded the fish are. Survivors may be stressed for some days, grow more slowly and be more likely to pick up infections, so watch them closely. Unless the cause is fixed, such as overstocking, overfeeding, too much manure or no aeration, the problem often returns at the next cloudy spell. The long-term outlook for the farm is good when daily dawn checks, careful feeding and a water or aeration backup become routine.

faqs.q: Why do my fish always gasp and die early in the morning, not in the afternoon?
faqs.a: During the day, the green algae in the water use sunlight to make oxygen, so levels usually rise through the afternoon. At night there is no sunlight, and the algae, fish and the bacteria rotting waste all use oxygen without any being made. So oxygen falls all night and is lowest just before sunrise. That is why dawn is the most dangerous time and the best time to check your pond.

faqs.q: My catfish survived but all my tilapia died. Why?
faqs.a: African catfish have a special breathing organ that lets them gulp air at the surface. They can survive in water with very little oxygen for longer than tilapia. Tilapia depend on oxygen dissolved in the water, so they suffocate first. If you see tilapia dying while catfish look fine, low oxygen is a strong suspect. Even catfish can die if oxygen stays very low, so don't rely on them as an all-clear.

faqs.q: Can I sell or eat fish that died from low oxygen?
faqs.a: Fish collected alive and still fresh during a crisis can be harvested, kept cool and used like normal fish, as long as no medicines have been given. Fish found already dead in the water, especially after several hours in warm weather, spoil fast and can cause food poisoning, so do not sell or eat them. Bury or dispose of them away from the pond.

faqs.q: Will adding salt, lime or medicine help my gasping fish?
faqs.a: No. None of these add oxygen to the water, and in an emergency some can make things worse or stress fish further. The fix is fresh, splashing water and aeration, plus stopping feeding. Antibiotics do not help low oxygen at all and should only be used if a vet diagnoses a bacterial infection afterwards. Lime and salt have specific uses in pond management, so ask your fisheries officer when and how to use them.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my pond oxygen is low if I do not have a meter?
faqs.a: Watch your fish at dawn. Fish at the surface gulping air, crowding at the inlet or refusing morning feed are warning signs. Also watch the water: a sudden change in colour, from green to brown, grey or very clear, a bad smell or scum may mean the algae are dying. Be extra careful after two or three cloudy days, in very hot weather or after heavy feeding. Ask your extension officer to test with a meter, and consider buying a simple test kit if you farm intensively.

faqs.q: How do I stop this happening again?
faqs.a: Look at what changed before the crisis. Often it is too many fish for the pond, too much feed or manure, cloudy weather, or the water supply stopping. Reduce stocking or harvest some fish, feed only what is eaten quickly, and cut back feed on dull days. Avoid overfertilising, and keep a fresh water source or aerator ready. Most importantly, check the pond every morning at first light. Desilting and drying the pond between cycles also reduces the rotting mud that uses up oxygen.

card.headline: Fish gasping with red-brown gills
card.look: Fish crowd at the surface or the water inlet, gulping air, and stop eating. The water may be cloudy, dark or smell rotten, and lifting a gill cover shows swollen, dark red or brownish gills instead of a clean bright red.
card.action: Stop feeding at once, add fresh clean water or aeration, and call your fisheries officer or aquatic vet to test the water today.

aka: New tank or new pond syndrome
Brown blood disease (when nitrite is also high)
detail.summary: Ammonia poisoning happens when fish waste and rotting feed build up faster than the pond or tank can break them down. Ammonia is a natural waste fish release through their gills, but when it collects in the water it burns the gills, stresses the fish and opens the door to infections. It is one of the most common causes of poor growth and sudden deaths on tilapia and catfish farms in Kenya. The good news is that it is mostly preventable with sensible feeding, the right number of fish and regular water checks.
detail.cause: Fish pass most of their waste as ammonia straight out through their gills, and more ammonia is released when uneaten feed, dead fish, manure or decaying plants rot in the water. In a healthy pond, helpful bacteria turn ammonia into nitrite and then into nitrate, which is much less harmful, and algae and plants also take some up. Trouble starts when there are too many fish, too much feed or too little clean water, so ammonia builds up faster than it is removed. Ammonia exists in two forms: a less harmful form and a very toxic gas-like form. The warmer the water and the higher the pH (how alkaline the water is), the more of the toxic form there is, so the same test reading can be far more dangerous on a hot afternoon. The toxic ammonia damages the delicate gill tissue, which swells, produces extra mucus and becomes red and inflamed, so the fish cannot take in oxygen properly or get rid of waste. It also harms the skin, fins, liver and kidneys and weakens the immune system. If nitrite also builds up, it enters the blood and stops it carrying oxygen, turning the blood and gills chocolate brown. Low oxygen usually goes hand in hand with poor water, so fish are hit by several stresses at once, and bacteria and parasites then attack the weakened fish.
spread: Overfeeding is the most common trigger: feed that is not eaten within a few minutes sinks, rots and releases ammonia.
Stocking too many fish for the size of the pond, tank or water flow means more waste than the water can handle.
Rotting material such as dead fish left in the pond, too much manure or fertiliser, and decaying weeds or grass add large amounts of ammonia.
Poor water exchange or slow flow, especially in liner ponds, concrete tanks and recirculating systems, allows waste to collect.
A sudden algae die-off after cloudy weather or a sharp temperature change releases ammonia and uses up oxygen at the same time.
New ponds, newly cleaned tanks or filters that have been washed with chlorinated water lack the helpful bacteria that break down ammonia.
Hot sunny afternoons and high pH, including after adding too much quicklime or hydrated lime, turn more ammonia into its toxic form.
It is not an infection and does not pass from fish to fish, but the secondary bacterial and parasite infections that follow can spread through shared water, nets and equipment.
detail.atRisk: All farmed fish can be affected, but tilapia and especially fingerlings and fry are sensitive, as are fish in hatcheries and nursery tanks. African catfish (Clarias) tolerate poor water better because they can breathe air, but they still suffer gill damage, poor growth and disease. Fish in small liner ponds, concrete tanks, raised tanks and recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS, where water is filtered and reused) are at higher risk because waste builds up quickly. Heavily stocked cages and ponds near the end of a production cycle, when fish are big and eating the most feed, are a common problem point. Risk rises in the hot dry months, during spells of cloudy weather that cause algae to crash, after heavy manuring, and when water supply drops in the dry season. Farms that feed by guesswork, use poor-quality feed that breaks up quickly, or rarely test their water are the most likely to see losses.

early: Fish eat less or ignore feed, and pellets are left floating or sinking uneaten.
Fish gather near the surface, the water inlet or aerator, gulping air, often worst in the early morning.
Fish are slow, sluggish or hang in one place instead of swimming actively.
Fish appear darker than usual or show uneven colour from stress.
Some fish rub or flash against the sides or bottom, a sign of gill and skin irritation.
The water looks cloudy, very green, brown or foamy, or smells sour, rotten or like a toilet.
Growth slows and fish at harvest are smaller than expected for their age.
advanced: Gills look swollen, dark red or blotchy, covered in thick mucus, or brown in colour when nitrite is also high.
Gill covers flare open and breathing is fast and laboured.
Fins look frayed, ragged or eroded, sometimes with red streaks or a white edge.
Red patches, bleeding spots or sores appear on the skin, often where bacteria have moved in.
Eyes look cloudy or bulging, and fish may swim on their side, spin or lose balance.
Fish lie on the bottom or float weakly and do not react when you approach.
Daily deaths begin, often bigger fish first, and can turn into a sudden mass die-off, especially at dawn.

lookalikes.name: Low dissolved oxygen
lookalikes.howToTell: Low oxygen also makes fish gasp at the surface, and the two often happen together. Pure oxygen shortage is usually worst just before sunrise and improves quickly once aeration or fresh water is added, and the gills may look pale rather than red and swollen. Only an oxygen test and an ammonia test can tell you which is driving the problem.

lookalikes.name: Nitrite poisoning (brown blood disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is part of the same poor-water problem but shows chocolate-brown gills and blood rather than bright red inflamed gills. It is common in new or overloaded systems where the bacteria have not caught up. A nitrite test confirms it.

lookalikes.name: Bacterial gill disease and columnaris
lookalikes.howToTell: Bacteria can cause swollen gills, white or yellow patches on gills, skin and mouth, and fin rot. These infections often follow poor water, but the water tests may be normal if the original trigger has passed. A vet needs to look at gill samples and may culture the bacteria.

lookalikes.name: Gill and skin parasites
lookalikes.howToTell: Parasites such as Trichodina and gill flukes cause flashing, rubbing, extra mucus and gasping. Unlike ammonia, the water tests are often fine. A vet or fisheries officer can see the parasites by looking at a gill or skin scraping under a microscope.

lookalikes.name: Chemical or pesticide poisoning
lookalikes.howToTell: Runoff from sprayed farms, cattle dips or car washing can cause sudden deaths of many fish of all sizes at once, sometimes with twitching or erratic swimming. Think of it if deaths follow rain, spraying or a new water source, and water tests for ammonia are normal.

detail.diagnosis: Diagnosis starts with testing the water, because the problem is in the water, not just the fish. A fisheries officer or aquatic vet will measure total ammonia, nitrite, pH, temperature and dissolved oxygen, and sometimes alkalinity, then use the pH and temperature to work out how much of the ammonia is in the toxic form. They will look at your stocking density, feeding records, water source and pond or tank set-up. They usually examine a few sick fish, lifting the gill cover to check gill colour and swelling, and may look at gill and skin scrapings under a microscope to rule out parasites. If infection is suspected, they may take samples for bacterial culture at a laboratory, such as a county or national veterinary lab or a KMFRI aquaculture centre, and sometimes tissue samples to examine gill damage. To help, keep a record of daily feed amounts, fish numbers and size, deaths per day, recent water changes, fertiliser or manure use and weather. Collect a water sample in a clean bottle rinsed with pond water, from mid-depth away from the inlet, and keep it cool but not frozen. If possible, bring a few live, sick fish in a bag of pond water rather than dead ones, as fish decay very fast. Have your own test kit results ready if you have taken them.
firstSteps: Stop feeding completely for now; less feed means less ammonia, and stressed fish cannot digest well anyway. Resume slowly and in small amounts once fish are eating and water improves.
Increase oxygen straight away by running aerators or pumps, splashing water in, or letting fresh water flow in; this helps fish cope while you fix the ammonia.
Do a partial water change with clean water of similar temperature, replacing only part of the water at a time rather than draining the pond, to avoid shocking the fish.
Remove dead and dying fish and any rotting feed, weeds or debris from the water at least twice a day and bury or burn them away from the water.
Test the water for ammonia, nitrite, pH and oxygen if you have a kit, and write down the results with the time and temperature.
Do not add quicklime, hydrated lime, fertiliser or manure now, because raising the pH makes ammonia more toxic and fertiliser adds more waste.
Do not add any medicines, antibiotics or chemicals to the water without advice from a vet or fisheries officer.
Avoid netting, grading, transporting or selling fish while they are stressed, and wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish.
Call your County Fisheries Officer, aquatic vet or a trusted agrovet with fish experience the same day, especially if deaths are rising.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that cures ammonia poisoning; the treatment is to fix the water and remove the cause. The vet or fisheries officer will guide you on how much water to exchange and how quickly, how to improve aeration, and how many fish to remove or harvest early to reduce the load. In tanks and recirculating systems they may advise cleaning or rebuilding the biological filter, adding a starter culture of helpful bacteria, or adjusting pH and alkalinity carefully. Where nitrite is high, they may recommend adding a measured amount of plain, non-iodised salt, because chloride helps block nitrite from entering the fish; the amount depends on your water and fish, so follow their advice. Products such as zeolite are sometimes sold to bind ammonia, but results in ponds vary and they do not replace water exchange. If fish have developed bacterial infections such as fin rot or ulcers, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic, usually as medicated feed, after confirming the infection. Antibiotics should only be used on a vet's prescription, as wrong use breeds resistant bacteria that harm fish and people, and drug-treated fish must not be sold or eaten until the withdrawal period on the prescription is over. Parasites, if found, are treated separately. Once the water is right, healthy fish usually start feeding again within days, though damaged gills take longer to heal.
prevention: Feed carefully: give only what the fish eat in a few minutes, split into two or more meals, and adjust the amount as fish grow using a feeding chart from your feed supplier or fisheries officer.
Reduce or skip feeding on very hot afternoons, cloudy or cold days, and when fish show little appetite, because uneaten feed quickly becomes ammonia.
Stock fish at the density recommended for your pond type, water supply and aeration, and harvest or thin out fish as they grow rather than overcrowding near harvest.
Test water regularly, ideally weekly and more often in tanks and RAS, for ammonia, nitrite, pH and oxygen, and keep written records so you can spot rising trends early.
Keep a steady supply of clean water and plan partial water changes, especially in the dry season and in liner ponds and tanks.
Use good-quality, water-stable feed that does not break up quickly, and store it dry and off the floor so mouldy or spoiled feed is not used.
Fertilise and manure ponds lightly and only on advice, keep water colour a moderate green, and remove excess weeds and decaying plants.
Remove dead fish daily, keep inlets and outlets clear, and for new ponds or tanks stock slowly so helpful bacteria have time to build up.
Never clean biofilters with chlorinated tap water, and use aerators or water flow to keep oxygen up, especially at night and at dawn.
detail.impact: Poor water quality is one of the biggest hidden costs on Kenyan fish farms. Even before fish die, ammonia stress slows growth, so fish take longer to reach market size and more feed is spent for every kilo of fish, and feed is already the largest cost in most tilapia and catfish enterprises. Stressed fish catch bacterial and parasite infections more easily, bringing more losses and treatment costs. When things go badly, a whole pond or tank can be lost in one night, wiping out months of feed, fingerlings and labour. Smaller, damaged or blemished fish fetch lower prices from buyers, hotels and markets. For farmers who borrowed to start or who sell into contracts, one bad die-off can make the season unprofitable. Regular testing and careful feeding cost far less than these losses.
detail.humanHealth: Ammonia in pond water is not a direct danger to people at the levels found in fish farms. The risk comes from what happens next: fish weakened by poor water often carry bacteria such as Aeromonas, which can infect cuts and wounds on hands, so wear gloves, wash well after handling sick or dead fish and do not handle them with open cuts. Do not sell or eat fish that were found dead or dying, as they spoil very quickly. If a vet prescribes antibiotics or other drugs, respect the withdrawal period fully before harvesting, selling or eating the fish, to avoid drug residues reaching consumers.
detail.outlook: If the problem is caught early and the water is corrected quickly, most fish recover well and start feeding again within a few days, although growth may be set back for a while. Mildly damaged gills can heal over a few weeks once water stays clean. The outlook is poorer when fish are already showing severe gill damage, sores, loss of balance or many daily deaths, when fry and fingerlings are affected, or when low oxygen and nitrite are also high. Fish that survive a serious episode can remain weaker and more prone to disease. The biggest factor in long-term success is fixing the root cause, such as overfeeding or overstocking, so the problem does not keep coming back.

faqs.q: Why do my fish die mostly early in the morning?
faqs.a: At night, algae and plants stop producing oxygen and instead use it up, as do fish and rotting waste. By dawn, oxygen is at its lowest, and fish already stressed by ammonia cannot cope. That is why you often find fish gasping or dead at sunrise. Aerating at night and early morning, feeding less and keeping the water cleaner all help.

faqs.q: How do I know if I am overfeeding?
faqs.a: If pellets are still floating or lying on the bottom several minutes after feeding, you are giving too much. Other signs are water that smells bad, turns very green or cloudy quickly, or foam on the surface. Feed small amounts, watch the fish eat, and stop when they slow down. Ask your feed supplier or fisheries officer for a feeding chart based on fish weight and water temperature.

faqs.q: Can I test the water myself?
faqs.a: Yes. Simple test kits for ammonia, nitrite and pH are sold in some agrovets and aquaculture suppliers, and oxygen meters are available for larger farms. Follow the instructions carefully and note the water temperature. A reading that rises week by week is an early warning even before fish look sick. If readings are high or you are unsure what they mean, share them with your fisheries officer.

faqs.q: Should I add lime to fix the problem?
faqs.a: Not during an ammonia problem without advice. Quicklime and hydrated lime raise the pH sharply, which turns more ammonia into its toxic form and can kill fish quickly. Agricultural lime is used to correct acidic or soft water, usually when preparing a pond, and only after testing. Let the fisheries officer guide any liming.

faqs.q: Can antibiotics save my fish?
faqs.a: Antibiotics do not remove ammonia or fix bad water, so they will not solve the main problem. They only help when a vet confirms a bacterial infection on top of the water problem, and they must be prescribed. Using them without need wastes money, encourages resistant bacteria and leaves residues, so fish cannot be sold until the withdrawal period ends.

faqs.q: Are the surviving fish safe to eat and sell?
faqs.a: Healthy-looking fish that recover after the water is corrected are generally safe to harvest, as ammonia itself does not stay in the flesh in a way that harms people. Do not sell fish found dead or dying, and if any drugs were used, wait for the full withdrawal period on the prescription. Harvest and chill fish quickly to keep quality good.
