card.headline: Bulging, cloudy eyes and spinning swimming
card.look: Tilapia with one or both eyes bulging out (pop-eye) or turning milky white, often with a swollen belly and dark skin. Sick fish swim in circles, spiral or spin near the surface, then sink or lie still, and dead fish appear day after day, often in the hottest weeks.
card.action: Reduce or stop feeding, remove dead fish every day, boost aeration and call a fish health officer or vet for laboratory confirmation before any treatment.

aka: Pop-eye disease (a common sign, not a separate disease)
detail.summary: Streptococcosis is a serious bacterial disease of farmed tilapia, caused mainly by Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus iniae. The bacteria spread through the blood and attack the brain and eyes, so sick fish swim abnormally, develop bulging or cloudy eyes, and die. It is one of the most damaging tilapia diseases worldwide, especially in warm water, and it often hits larger fish close to harvest, when the farmer has already spent most of the money on feed. Early recognition and good water management can limit the losses.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Streptococcus bacteria, mainly Streptococcus agalactiae (sometimes called Group B Strep) and Streptococcus iniae. These bacteria can live in pond water, mud and in apparently healthy carrier fish without causing obvious problems. When fish are stressed, for example by hot water, low oxygen, high ammonia from too much feed and waste, overcrowding or rough handling, their defences weaken and the bacteria enter the body, usually through the gut, gills or small skin wounds. Once in the blood (septicaemia means bacteria spreading in the blood), they multiply and travel to the brain, eyes, kidney, spleen and heart. Infection of the brain and its covering (meningoencephalitis) is what causes the spinning, circling and loss of balance. Infection inside and behind the eye causes fluid and swelling, so the eye bulges out (exophthalmia, or pop-eye) and the cornea turns cloudy. Fluid may also build up in the belly, making it look swollen. Some outbreaks are sudden with many deaths; others are slow, with a few fish dying every day for weeks.
spread: Through the water: sick and dying fish shed huge numbers of bacteria, which spread through the pond, and from cage to cage in lakes and dams by water currents.
Dead and dying fish left in the pond or cage, because healthy fish nibble on them and swallow the bacteria.
Bringing in infected or carrier fingerlings from a hatchery that has the disease, which is one of the commonest ways it reaches a new farm.
Shared nets, buckets, hapas, boats, transport tanks and boots that move from an infected pond or cage to a clean one without cleaning and drying.
Water flowing from an infected pond into another pond, or wild fish and birds carrying infected fish between ponds.

Triggers that turn a hidden infection into an outbreak: water temperature above roughly 27–28 °C, low dissolved oxygen, high ammonia or nitrite, overstocking, overfeeding, and stress from grading, sorting, netting or transport.
detail.atRisk: Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and other tilapia species are most at risk, along with some other warm-water fish. In Kenya and East Africa the highest risk is in intensive systems: cage farms on Lake Victoria and large dams, heavily stocked liner and concrete ponds, and recirculating tanks, where many fish share the same water. Streptococcus agalactiae often strikes larger, fast-growing fish (from fingerling grow-out up to market size), while Streptococcus iniae can also affect younger fish. Outbreaks are most common in the hot, dry months before the long rains and during any spell of hot, still weather, when water warms up and oxygen falls. Shallow ponds, ponds with no shade or aeration, ponds receiving heavy feeding, and farms that buy fingerlings from many different sources are at greater risk. Earthen ponds with low stocking can still be affected, but outbreaks there tend to be smaller.

early: Fish eat less than usual and leave pellets uneaten, or the shoal is slow to come up at feeding time.
A few fish swim slowly or alone near the edges, at the surface or near water inlets, separate from the shoal.
Some fish turn darker in colour than the others.
Odd swimming in a few fish: short bursts of spinning, swimming on their side, tail-chasing or 'whirling' when disturbed.
One eye starting to bulge slightly or looking hazy, and sometimes small red spots around the eye, mouth, fin bases or gill covers.
A small but steady rise in the number of dead fish collected each morning, often larger fish.
advanced: Marked pop-eye: one or both eyes bulging far out of the head, sometimes with blood inside the eye.
Eyes turning milky white or opaque, and some fish becoming blind; eyes may burst or be lost.
Strong spinning, spiral or C-shaped swimming, fish floating head-up or belly-up, then sinking and lying on the bottom.
Swollen, soft belly from fluid build-up, sometimes with a red, swollen vent (anal opening).
Curved or bent body in some fish, and bleeding at the base of fins or on the gill covers.
Daily deaths that keep going for days or weeks, or a sudden heavy die-off during very hot weather.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or fish health officer starts by looking at the pond or cage, the fish behaviour, the pattern of deaths, the water temperature and the water quality. Pop-eye with cloudy eyes and spinning in warm water strongly suggests streptococcosis, but other diseases look similar, so laboratory confirmation is important. The lab takes swabs or tissue from the brain, kidney, spleen and eye of freshly sick fish and grows the bacteria on culture plates; Streptococcus shows as small round bacteria in chains under the microscope. PCR (a DNA test) can identify the exact species, and an antibiotic sensitivity test shows which drugs will actually work, which is very valuable because resistance varies. Histology (looking at thin slices of tissue) may also be done. In Kenya, contact your County Fisheries or County Veterinary office, or institutions such as KMFRI (Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute) and university or government veterinary labs. To help, the farmer should send 3–5 live sick fish (showing signs, not long dead) in a bag of pond water with air, or freshly dead fish chilled on ice but not frozen; record water temperature, oxygen if you can measure it, stocking numbers, feed used, recent handling or new fish, and daily death counts.
firstSteps: Reduce feeding sharply or stop for a few days, because sick fish eat little, leftover feed rots and lowers oxygen, and the bacteria spread more easily when fish crowd at feeding; ask your fish health officer how long.

Remove dead and dying fish at least once a day, and bury them deep with lime away from water or burn them; never throw them back into the lake, a stream or another pond, and never feed them to other fish.
Improve water conditions: increase aeration or paddlewheel time, add fresh, clean, cooler water if available, add shade, and check temperature, oxygen and ammonia, especially early in the morning.
Stop all handling, grading, sorting, netting and transport of fish from affected ponds or cages until the vet advises, because stress makes the outbreak worse.
Do not move fish, water, nets or equipment from the affected unit to healthy ones; use separate nets and buckets, and wash and sun-dry equipment after use.
Wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish, avoid getting fish spines into cuts, and wash hands well with soap afterwards.
Keep a written record of daily deaths, signs seen, water temperature and feeding, and keep a few freshly sick fish for the lab.
Call a vet or fish health officer quickly, and do not buy or use antibiotics from the agrovet on your own, as the wrong drug wastes money and builds resistance.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be decided and prescribed by a vet or qualified fish health professional, ideally after the bacteria have been identified and a sensitivity test done. Fish are usually treated with antibiotics mixed into feed (medicated feed), because injecting every fish is not practical in grow-out. Drug classes used internationally for tilapia streptococcosis include florfenicol, amoxicillin and other penicillins, and macrolides such as erythromycin; older drugs like oxytetracycline often work poorly against Streptococcus. Which drugs are legally allowed for food fish differs by country, so your vet will advise what is approved in Kenya. A major problem is that very sick fish stop eating, so they do not take in the medicated feed; treatment works best when started early, while most fish are still feeding. Antibiotics do not repair damaged eyes or brains, so blind or badly affected fish often still die or grow poorly. Putting antibiotics directly into pond or lake water is wasteful, pollutes the environment and encourages antimicrobial resistance, so it should not be done. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, a set time after treatment before fish can be harvested, sold or eaten, and this must be followed strictly. Alongside any drug, the vet will insist on better water quality, lower stocking, less stress and daily removal of dead fish, because these are what actually stop the outbreak. Expect deaths to continue for some days even with good treatment.
prevention: Buy fingerlings only from licensed, reputable hatcheries with a good health record, ask about past disease problems, and avoid mixing fish from many different sources.
Quarantine new fish in a separate pond or tank for a few weeks where possible, watching them for abnormal swimming, eye changes or deaths before mixing them with your stock.
Keep stocking density within recommended levels for your system (pond, liner, cage or tank), since overcrowding is one of the biggest triggers.
Manage water quality: aerate, exchange water, avoid overfeeding, remove sludge, and measure dissolved oxygen, temperature and ammonia regularly, especially in hot months.
Protect fish from heat: use deeper ponds, partial shade, and extra aeration during hot spells, and in cages choose sites with good depth and water flow.
Avoid grading, sorting, netting and transporting fish during the hottest part of the day or the hottest season; do it in cool early mornings and handle fish gently.
Feed good-quality, properly stored feed in the right amounts, and reduce feeding when water is very hot or oxygen is low.
Remove dead fish daily, use separate equipment for each pond or cage group, disinfect and sun-dry nets and buckets, and between cycles drain, dry and lime earthen ponds.

Ask your fish health officer about vaccination: inactivated Streptococcus vaccines are used in tilapia in some countries, but availability and registration in Kenya are limited, so check what is approved and suited to the local strains.
detail.impact: Streptococcosis can cause heavy losses on Kenyan tilapia farms. Because it often strikes larger fish near market size, the farmer loses fish on which most of the feed money, the biggest cost in fish farming, has already been spent. Cage farms on Lake Victoria and intensive pond or tank units can lose a large share of a cycle in a bad outbreak, while smaller ponds may see a steady trickle of deaths that quietly eats into profit. Survivors often grow slowly, convert feed poorly, and fish with damaged eyes or bent bodies fetch lower prices or cannot be sold at all. Extra costs come from lab tests, medicated feed, aeration, fuel or electricity, and lost time. Fish under antibiotic withdrawal cannot be sold, which can delay harvest and upset contracts with traders, hotels or supermarkets. Repeated outbreaks can damage a farm's or hatchery's reputation and discourage buyers.
detail.humanHealth: Streptococcus iniae and some strains of Streptococcus agalactiae can infect people, though this is uncommon. Most human cases reported worldwide involved people who handled or cleaned live or raw fish and got a cut or a fish-spine prick on the hand, leading to painful skin and soft tissue infection; rarely the infection spreads more widely. A particular strain of Streptococcus agalactiae has been linked to eating raw freshwater fish in parts of Asia. To protect yourself, wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish, cover any cuts, avoid spine pricks, and wash hands well with soap and water. Cook fish thoroughly and do not eat raw fish from an affected farm. Do not sell or eat visibly sick fish. If you develop a red, swollen, painful hand or fever after handling fish, see a doctor and mention fish contact. If antibiotics are used, respect the withdrawal period so that drug residues do not end up in food.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early the problem is spotted and how quickly stress is reduced. When deaths are noticed early, feeding is cut, water quality improved, dead fish removed daily and the vet confirms the cause and prescribes effective treatment, many fish in the pond or cage can be saved and deaths can slow within days to weeks. Individual fish with bulging or white eyes and strong spinning rarely recover fully, and blind survivors grow poorly. Outbreaks in very hot weather, crowded cages or ponds with low oxygen tend to be the most severe. Surviving fish can carry the bacteria, so the disease can return when the next stress or hot season comes, unless the farm improves biosecurity, stocking and water management.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell fish from a pond with streptococcosis?
faqs.a: Do not eat or sell fish that are visibly sick, have bulging or white eyes, or were found dead. Healthy-looking fish from an affected pond should be handled with gloves and cooked thoroughly, never eaten raw. If the fish have been given antibiotics, you must wait until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed before harvesting or selling any fish. Ask your fish health officer for advice before an emergency harvest.

faqs.q: Why does this disease appear when the weather is hot?
faqs.a: Streptococcus bacteria grow faster in warm water, and outbreaks in tilapia are strongly linked to water temperatures above about 27–28 °C. Hot water also holds less oxygen, and fish eat and excrete more, so ammonia rises. Together these stress the fish and weaken their defences, allowing hidden bacteria to cause disease. That is why deeper water, shade, aeration and careful feeding matter most in the hottest months.

faqs.q: Can I just buy antibiotics from the agrovet and put them in the pond?
faqs.a: No. Pouring antibiotics into pond or lake water wastes most of the drug, harms the environment and helps bacteria become resistant, so the drugs stop working for fish and even people. Many common antibiotics also work poorly against Streptococcus. Treatment should be prescribed by a vet, usually as medicated feed, ideally after a lab test shows which drug works, and the withdrawal period must be followed.

faqs.q: Should I empty the pond and start again?
faqs.a: Not always. In many outbreaks, cutting feed, improving water and removing dead fish daily, with vet-guided treatment, can save much of the stock. If losses are very heavy or the fish are near market size, your vet may suggest an early harvest of healthy fish. At the end of the cycle, draining, drying and liming an earthen pond, and cleaning and drying cages and nets, helps reduce the bacteria before restocking.

faqs.q: Will the disease come back next cycle?
faqs.a: It can, because the bacteria may survive in carrier fish, mud, equipment and nearby farms, especially in shared lakes. Your chances improve if you buy fingerlings from a reliable hatchery, avoid overstocking, keep good water quality, handle fish only in cool weather, remove dead fish daily and keep equipment separate. Keeping records of each outbreak helps you and your fish health officer spot risky times and conditions.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for tilapia streptococcosis in Kenya?
faqs.a: Vaccines against Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus iniae are used for tilapia in some other countries, usually given by injection or by dipping fish. Their availability and registration in Kenya are limited, and a vaccine works best when it matches the local strain. Ask your County Fisheries officer, vet or KMFRI whether an approved vaccine is available, and remember vaccination only works well alongside good management.

streptococcosis.imagePrompt: Close-up side view of a live Nile tilapia held just above pond water, showing one strongly bulging cloudy white eye and a slightly swollen belly, with a murky green pond in the soft-focus background, natural daylight, realistic photograph.
streptococcosis.seoDescription: Streptococcosis in tilapia: pop-eye, cloudy eyes, spinning and deaths in warm water. Learn signs, first steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan fish farms.

card.headline: Grey-white saddle patch across fish back
card.look: Pale grey, white or yellowish patches appear on the skin, often in a band across the back behind the top fin like a saddle. The fins look ragged and eaten away, and the gills may show pale or brown dead areas.
card.action: Stop all handling and movement of fish, check and improve water oxygen and quality straight away, and call your County Fisheries Officer or a fish vet.

detail.summary: Columnaris is a bacterial disease of the skin, fins and gills of freshwater fish, caused by Flavobacterium columnare and closely related bacteria. It usually strikes a few days after fish have been handled, graded, transported or stressed by poor water, warm temperatures or crowding. In Kenya it affects tilapia, African catfish, trout and ornamental fish. It can spread through a pond or tank quickly and kill many fish, especially fingerlings, so early action on water quality and stress makes a big difference.
detail.cause: The cause is a long, thin, rod-shaped bacterium called Flavobacterium columnare. Scientists have recently split it into several closely related species, but they cause the same disease and farmers can treat them as one problem. These bacteria live naturally in most freshwater ponds, rivers, dams and on the fish themselves, so their presence alone does not mean disease. Trouble starts when fish are stressed or their protective skin slime (mucus) is damaged, for example by rough netting, crowding in transport tanks, low oxygen, high ammonia (a toxic waste from fish droppings and rotting feed) or warm water. The bacteria then stick to the skin, fins and gills, multiply and produce enzymes that break down tissue. On the skin this forms pale, dead patches that may become shallow ulcers. On the fins the edges rot away. On the gills, which are the organs fish use to breathe, the bacteria destroy the delicate gill filaments so the fish cannot take in enough oxygen or get rid of waste. Gill damage is often what kills the fish, sometimes before skin lesions are obvious. Damaged skin also lets water and salts leak in and out of the body and lets other germs in, so secondary infections with bacteria such as Aeromonas or water moulds are common.
spread: Handling, netting, grading, sorting and transporting fish rub off the protective mucus and are the most common trigger, with disease often showing two to five days later.
The bacteria pass from fish to fish through the water, so one sick fish in a crowded tank or pond can quickly infect the rest.
Dead and dying fish left in the water release large numbers of bacteria and should be seen as a major source of infection.
Shared nets, buckets, hapas, transport tanks and boots carry the bacteria from one pond to another when they are not cleaned and dried.
Buying in fingerlings from a hatchery with poor hygiene, or mixing new fish with your stock without quarantine, can bring in the disease.
Warm water, especially in the hot dry months before the long rains and in shallow ponds or plastic-lined tanks in full sun, favours fast growth of the bacteria.
Poor water quality such as low dissolved oxygen, high ammonia or nitrite, heavy algae die-off, muddy water after heavy rain and overfeeding all weaken fish and make outbreaks more likely.
Water flowing from an infected pond into others, or from rivers and dams with wild fish, can carry the bacteria onto the farm.
detail.atRisk: All freshwater fish can be affected, but in Kenya the disease is most often seen in Nile tilapia, African catfish (Clarias, locally called kambare), rainbow trout in the cold-water farms of Central and Rift Valley highlands, and aquarium or ornamental fish such as goldfish and koi. Fry and fingerlings are the most vulnerable because their skin and gills are delicate, but adult brood fish also suffer after spawning or handling. Risk is highest just after stocking, transport, grading, harvesting part of a pond, or treatment baths. Warm conditions increase risk, so tilapia and catfish ponds in hot lowland areas, shallow ponds and tanks in direct sun, and trout farms during unusually warm spells are especially exposed. Intensive systems such as high-density tanks, recirculating systems and cages, as well as small backyard ponds that are overstocked, overfed or poorly aerated, see more outbreaks than well-managed, lightly stocked earthen ponds.

early: Fish gather near the water inlet or at the surface and gulp air, especially in the early morning when oxygen is lowest.
Fish eat less or stop coming to feed, and leftover pellets are seen in the pond.
Small pale, greyish or whitish spots or patches appear on the skin, head, mouth or around the fins, sometimes with a yellowish tinge.
Fin edges look frayed, white-edged or slightly eaten away, especially the tail and top fin.
The body may look dull or covered in extra slime, and fish may rub against the pond sides or bottom.
Gills, when gently checked on a caught fish, may have pale, whitish or brownish-yellow patches instead of a healthy deep red colour.
A few fish die each day, often those that were handled most or are weakest.
advanced: A clear pale or grey band of damaged skin forms across the back behind the dorsal (top) fin, giving the classic saddle-back look.
Patches turn into shallow, open sores with yellowish or orange edges, and scales may fall off around them.
Fins are badly eroded down to the base, and the tail may be almost gone.
White, fluffy-looking or cotton-like growth appears around the mouth and lips, which is why it is called cotton-mouth.
Gills are badly eaten away, swollen or covered in yellow-brown debris, and fish breathe fast with flared gill covers.
Fish become weak, swim slowly or lie near the edges, and lose balance.
Deaths rise sharply over a few days, and in fingerlings a large part of the batch can be lost if nothing is changed.

lookalikes.name: Water mould (Saprolegnia, fungal infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Water mould forms soft, fluffy, cotton-wool tufts that float out in the water and are usually pure white or turn brown-green as they trap dirt. Columnaris patches are flatter, greyer or yellowish and lie on the skin rather than standing out as long fibres. The two often occur together, so a vet or fisheries officer using a microscope is the reliable way to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: White spot disease (Ich, Ichthyophthirius parasite)
lookalikes.howToTell: White spot shows as many tiny, separate white dots like grains of salt or sugar scattered over the body and fins. Columnaris causes larger, spreading patches, saddle-shaped bands and rotting fins rather than neat pinhead spots.

lookalikes.name: Motile Aeromonas septicaemia (red sore or haemorrhagic disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Aeromonas infection usually causes red, bloody-looking ulcers, red streaks on fins and belly, a swollen belly and bulging eyes. Columnaris lesions are mainly pale, grey or yellowish with eroded fins and gills. Aeromonas can also invade columnaris sores, so mixed signs are possible and lab tests help.

lookalikes.name: Water quality problems (low oxygen, ammonia or nitrite poisoning)
lookalikes.howToTell: When the water itself is the problem, many fish of all sizes gasp at the surface at once, often at dawn or after an algae crash, and there may be no skin patches at all. Columnaris usually starts in a few fish with visible skin, fin or gill lesions and spreads over days. Testing the water with a simple kit settles the question, and poor water can trigger columnaris, so both may be present.

detail.diagnosis: A vet, fisheries officer or aquaculture laboratory usually starts by asking about recent handling, stocking, transport, feeding and water temperature, and by watching how the fish behave in the pond. They then catch a few sick but still living fish and look closely at the skin, fins and gills. The quickest test is a wet mount: a small scraping of slime or gill tissue is put on a glass slide and looked at under a microscope. Columnaris bacteria appear as long, thin, gliding rods that gather into characteristic columns or haystack-like clumps, which gives the disease its name. To confirm, samples can be grown on special low-nutrient culture plates, where the bacteria form yellowish, spreading colonies, and some laboratories use PCR (a test that detects the germ's genetic material) to identify the exact species. Labs may also test which antibiotics will work, which is important for responsible use. Water will be tested for temperature, dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite and pH. In Kenya, help can be sought from your County Fisheries or Veterinary Officer, the Kenya Fisheries Service, KMFRI aquaculture research centres such as Sagana, and university or government veterinary laboratories. To prepare, keep a written record of when signs began, daily deaths, feeding, recent handling or new stock and any treatments used. Have five or more live, sick fish ready in a clean bucket of pond water with an air stone if possible, because fish that have been dead for hours are of little use for testing. Note water test results and the source of your fingerlings.
firstSteps: Stop all netting, grading, sorting, sampling and transport of fish from the affected pond or tank, because every handling makes the disease worse and spreads it.
Improve oxygen immediately by running aerators or paddle wheels, increasing water flow, or adding fresh, clean, well-oxygenated water of a similar temperature to the pond.
Test the water for oxygen, ammonia, nitrite, pH and temperature if you have a kit, and write the results down to share with the fisheries officer or vet.
Reduce feeding or stop it for a day or two, since sick fish eat little and uneaten feed rots, lowers oxygen and raises ammonia.
Provide shade over small ponds and tanks during hot weather, for example with shade net, to help keep the water cooler.
Remove dead and dying fish at least once or twice a day, and bury them deeply with lime or burn them away from water sources, rather than throwing them into rivers or feeding them to other animals.
Keep separate nets, buckets and boots for the sick pond, and wash and sun-dry or disinfect equipment before using it anywhere else on the farm.
Do not move fish from the sick pond into other ponds and do not sell or give away live fish until the problem is under control.
Record daily deaths, feeding, water results and any changes in behaviour, and call your County Fisheries Officer or a fish vet for advice before using any chemical or medicine.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment of columnaris always begins with fixing the underlying stress, because the bacteria are already present in most water and the disease returns if conditions stay poor. A vet or fisheries officer will usually advise better aeration, partial water changes, lower stocking density, reduced feeding, removal of organic waste and, where possible, cooler water. Depending on the species, the system and what is legally available, they may advise external treatments such as baths or dips using salt, potassium permanganate or hydrogen peroxide to reduce bacteria on the skin and gills. These chemicals can easily harm or kill fish if the strength, water quality or timing is wrong, and some species, especially catfish and fry, are very sensitive, so they must only be used under professional guidance and never by guesswork. In severe or spreading outbreaks, a vet may prescribe antibiotics mixed into feed, such as oxytetracycline or florfenicol, where these are registered for fish. Medicated feed only works if fish are still eating, so it is most useful early in an outbreak. Antibiotics must be prescribed by a vet, ideally after a lab test shows which drug will work, and the full course must be followed. Using antibiotics casually in ponds wastes money, pollutes the water, harms beneficial bacteria and builds antimicrobial resistance, where medicines stop working for fish and people. Any drug used has a withdrawal period, a set time during which treated fish must not be harvested or sold for food, and this must be strictly respected. Farmers should expect losses to slow within days once water quality improves and treatment starts, but some badly damaged fish will still die, and survivors need time and good conditions to heal their skin and fins.
prevention: Handle fish as little and as gently as possible, use soft knotless nets, keep fish in water rather than in the air, and avoid grading or moving them during the hottest part of the day or season.
Before and after transport or stocking, give fish clean, well-aerated water, avoid overcrowding in transport containers and allow them to settle without feeding heavily for the first day.
Keep stocking density within what your pond, tank or cage and aeration can support, as advised by your fisheries extension officer.
Maintain good water quality by testing regularly, using aeration where needed, exchanging water, removing sludge between cycles and avoiding sudden changes in temperature or pH.
Feed a good-quality, correctly sized fish feed in amounts the fish clear within a few minutes, and store feed dry and cool so it does not go mouldy or lose vitamins, which weakens immunity.
Buy fingerlings only from certified, reputable hatcheries, ask about their disease history, and quarantine new fish in a separate tank for observation before mixing them with your stock.
Keep separate equipment for each pond or disinfect nets, buckets and hapas between uses, and dry ponds and treat them with agricultural lime between production cycles.
Provide shade or deeper water in hot areas, and plan harvesting, grading and restocking for cooler months or early mornings.
Remove dead fish every day, keep records of deaths and water quality, and act early when you notice fish gasping, off-feed or showing pale patches.
detail.impact: Columnaris can cause heavy losses on Kenyan fish farms, especially among fingerlings just after stocking, which means farmers lose the money spent on seed, transport and early feed. Even when deaths are moderate, sick fish stop eating and grow slowly, so harvests are delayed and fish reach market below the expected size. Scarred, fin-damaged fish fetch lower prices or may be rejected by buyers, hotels and supermarkets that want clean-looking fish. Treatment, extra aeration, water pumping and lab tests add cost, and where antibiotics are used, the withdrawal period can delay sales. Hatcheries that suffer repeated outbreaks lose customers and reputation. For smallholders who joined fish farming through county or national programmes, a single bad outbreak can wipe out a season's profit, which is why prevention through gentle handling and good water management pays off.
detail.humanHealth: Columnaris is not considered a disease that infects people, and properly cooked fish from an affected pond is not known to cause the illness in humans. However, sick and dying fish often carry other germs, so wear gloves or wash hands well with soap after handling them and cover any cuts on your hands. Do not eat or sell fish that died of disease. If your fish have been treated with antibiotics or chemicals, strictly follow the withdrawal period given by the vet before harvesting, eating or selling them, because drug residues in fish meat can harm consumers and contribute to antimicrobial resistance.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mostly on how early the problem is spotted and how quickly the stress behind it is corrected. When water quality, oxygen and crowding are fixed early and professional treatment follows, losses often slow down within days and most fish recover, with fins and skin regrowing over the following weeks. Outbreaks in fry and fingerlings, those with severe gill damage, and those in very warm or badly polluted water carry a poorer outlook, and many affected fish may die. Fish that survive can carry the bacteria and remain at risk of relapse if stressed again, so continued good management is essential. Repeated outbreaks on the same farm are a sign that handling, stocking density or water management needs to change.

faqs.q: Why do my fish get sick a few days after I move or sort them?
faqs.a: Netting and handling rub off the protective slime layer and cause tiny injuries to the skin and gills, and crowding during transport adds stress and lowers oxygen. Columnaris bacteria already live in most ponds and take advantage of this damage, so signs often appear two to five days later. Gentle handling, moving fish in cool parts of the day, avoiding overcrowded containers and giving clean, well-aerated water afterwards greatly reduce the risk.

faqs.q: Is this the same as fungus on my fish?
faqs.a: Not exactly. Columnaris is a bacterial disease that causes flat grey, white or yellowish patches, saddle-shaped bands and rotting fins and gills. True fungus, more correctly a water mould called Saprolegnia, forms long fluffy cotton-like tufts. The two can look alike and often appear together because water mould grows on damaged skin. A quick microscope check by a fisheries officer or vet tells them apart, and the right treatment differs, so it is worth getting it confirmed.

faqs.q: Can I just add antibiotics from the agrovet to the pond water?
faqs.a: No. Pouring antibiotics into pond water is wasteful, rarely reaches the right level to work, pollutes the environment and kills useful bacteria in the pond. It also builds antimicrobial resistance, so medicines stop working in future for fish, livestock and people. If antibiotics are needed, a vet will prescribe a suitable product, usually in feed, and tell you the withdrawal period before the fish can be eaten or sold. Fixing water quality and stress is always the first and most important step.

faqs.q: Is salt safe to use for columnaris?
faqs.a: Salt baths are a common treatment for many freshwater fish and can help reduce bacteria on the skin and support the fish's salt balance. But the correct strength and time vary with species, fish size and water conditions, and catfish, fry and some ornamental fish can be harmed by the wrong strength. Ask your fisheries officer or a fish vet to guide you, test on a few fish first if advised, and always watch fish closely during any bath.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell fish from a pond with columnaris?
faqs.a: Columnaris is not known to infect people, so healthy-looking fish from the pond that have not received any medicine can be eaten after proper cleaning and cooking. Do not eat or sell fish that died of disease or look badly diseased, as other germs may be present and buyers will reject them. If any antibiotic or chemical treatment was used, you must wait the full withdrawal period your vet gives before harvesting for food.

faqs.q: Will the disease come back after the outbreak ends?
faqs.a: It can. The bacteria stay in the water and on surviving fish, so any new stress such as hot weather, overcrowding, low oxygen or rough handling can trigger another outbreak. Between cycles, drain and dry the pond, remove sludge and apply agricultural lime, clean all equipment, buy fingerlings from a reliable hatchery and keep stocking and feeding at sensible levels. Regular water testing and gentle handling are the best protection.

columnaris.imagePrompt: A live Nile tilapia swimming in clear shallow pond water, showing a distinct pale grey-white saddle-shaped band of damaged skin across its back just behind the dorsal fin and slightly frayed fin edges, natural daylight, realistic close-up photograph.
columnaris.seoDescription: Columnaris in tilapia, catfish and trout: spot grey-white saddle patches and rotting fins early, fix water quality, act fast and prevent outbreaks in Kenya.

card.headline: White cotton-wool tufts on skin and eggs
card.look: Fluffy white or grey patches, like wet cotton wool, grow on the fish's body, fins, gills or around wounds. In hatcheries, eggs become covered in a fuzzy white halo and may clump together. Older patches often turn brown or greenish as they trap mud and algae.
card.action: Remove dead fish and dead eggs at once, check and improve water quality, stop all unnecessary handling, and call your County Fisheries Officer or a vet with fish experience for advice.

aka: Cotton wool disease (also used loosely for a bacterial disease, columnaris)
detail.summary: Saprolegniasis is an infection caused by water moulds, mainly Saprolegnia, that grow as cotton-wool-like tufts on the skin, fins, gills and eggs of fish. It almost always attacks fish that are already injured, stressed or weak, and dead or unfertilised eggs in hatcheries. It matters because it can spread from dead eggs to healthy ones and wipe out a batch, and in ponds it can turn small wounds into deep sores that kill fish. In Kenya it is most often seen during the cold months and in highland farms, after rough handling, transport or spawning.
detail.cause: Saprolegnia is a water mould. It looks and behaves like a fungus, but scientists class it as an oomycete, a separate group of organisms. It lives naturally in almost all fresh water, ponds, rivers and tanks, feeding on dead plant and animal matter. Healthy fish are protected by a layer of slime (mucus) and intact skin and scales, so the mould usually cannot get a hold. When that protective layer is damaged, for example by netting, rough handling, fighting, bird attacks, parasites, bacterial sores or poor water, the mould's tiny swimming spores settle on the damaged spot and germinate. They grow fine threads (called hyphae) that spread across the skin and push into the flesh underneath. This destroys the skin surface, so the fish loses body salts and takes in too much water, which upsets its internal balance. If the gills are affected, the fish struggles to breathe. On eggs, the mould first grows on dead or unfertilised eggs, then its threads spread out and smother nearby healthy eggs, cutting off oxygen. Cool water favours the mould and also slows the fish's immune system, which is why the problem peaks when temperatures drop.
spread: Spores are already present in almost all fresh water, so the disease is triggered mainly by injury and stress rather than simply 'caught' from another farm.
Rough handling during netting, sorting, grading, weighing or transport scrapes off slime and scales and creates entry points for the mould.
Sudden drops in water temperature, such as during the cold season (roughly June to August) or when cold rain or borehole water floods a pond, weaken the fish and favour mould growth.
Dead fish and dead or unfertilised eggs left in the water grow large amounts of mould and release huge numbers of spores that then attack live fish and eggs.
Poor water quality, including low oxygen, high ammonia from overfeeding or overstocking, and dirty water full of organic matter, stresses fish and feeds the mould.
Wounds from fighting, cannibalism in catfish, predator birds, otters, monitor lizards and parasites such as anchor worm or lice open the skin for infection.
Spawning stress and hormone-induced breeding leave broodstock thin-skinned and run-down, so they often develop mould after stripping.
Contaminated nets, buckets, hatchery trays and water shared between tanks can carry spores and infected material from one unit to another.
detail.atRisk: Fish eggs and newly hatched fry in hatcheries are at the highest risk, especially catfish and trout eggs incubated in trays or jars where dead eggs are not removed. Rainbow trout farmed in the cold highland rivers around Mount Kenya, the Aberdares and parts of the Rift Valley are very susceptible because their water is cool all year. Nile tilapia and African catfish in ponds are mostly affected during the cold season, in high-altitude counties, and after handling, transport or stocking. Broodstock after spawning, fingerlings just delivered from a hatchery, and fish in overstocked or poorly managed ponds and tanks are all more likely to suffer. Farms with muddy, unmanaged ponds, little water exchange, overfeeding, or frequent harvesting and sorting see more cases.

early: Small white or grey fluffy spots, like a thin layer of cotton wool, appear on the skin, fins, tail or around the mouth and eyes.
The fluffy growth often starts at the edge of a wound, a damaged fin or a spot where scales have been lost after netting.
When the fish is lifted out of water the tufts collapse into a slimy, flat, greyish film, then fluff up again when put back.
Affected fish may rub against the pond sides or bottom and swim alone near the edges or the water inlet.
Fish eat less than usual and react slowly when feed is thrown in.
In hatchery trays or jars, dead eggs turn opaque white and develop a fine fuzzy halo of threads around them.
advanced: The patches spread and join into large areas covering the body, head or gills, sometimes looking like a woolly coat.
Older tufts turn brown, grey or greenish because they trap mud, algae and debris.
Fins become ragged and eroded, and pale or reddish sores appear under the mould when it comes away.
Infected gills look pale and clogged with fluffy growth, and the fish gasps at the surface.
Fish lose balance, lie on their side, stop feeding completely and become thin.
Deaths increase over several days, usually among fish that were already injured or weak.
In hatcheries, mould threads join eggs together into fuzzy mats, and healthy eggs inside the clump die.

lookalikes.name: Columnaris (bacterial 'cotton wool' or saddleback disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Columnaris is caused by bacteria, not mould. Patches are usually flatter, yellowish-white or greyish and often form a band across the back (a 'saddle'), with mouth and gill rot. It is more common in warm water, while Saprolegnia favours cool water. Under a microscope, a vet or fisheries officer sees bacteria instead of the long branching threads of mould, and the two are treated differently.

lookalikes.name: White spot (Ich, Ichthyophthirius)
lookalikes.howToTell: White spot shows as many small, separate, pinhead-sized white dots scattered over the body and fins, like grains of salt or sugar. There is no fluffy, hairy growth. Saprolegnia forms larger soft tufts, usually starting at a wound.

lookalikes.name: Excess mucus from poor water or parasites
lookalikes.howToTell: Fish irritated by ammonia, low pH or skin parasites may produce a cloudy, greyish slime layer over the whole body. This film is smooth and not fluffy, and it does not form cotton-like threads in the water. A skin scraping under a microscope helps tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Dead or unfertilised eggs without mould
lookalikes.howToTell: Dead eggs turn white and opaque but at first are smooth and clean. Only when Saprolegnia grows on them do they get a fuzzy halo of fine threads. Both should be removed quickly, because clean dead eggs soon become mouldy.

detail.diagnosis: A vet, County Fisheries Officer or aquaculture specialist usually suspects Saprolegnia from the typical cotton-wool appearance, the cool season and a recent history of handling, transport or spawning. To confirm, they take a small sample of the fluffy material or a skin scraping and look at it under a microscope: water mould shows long, branching threads without cross-walls, often with spore sacs at the tips. This also rules out bacteria such as columnaris and parasites, which often occur at the same time. Samples may be sent to a laboratory such as a county veterinary lab or KMFRI (Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute) for culture and to identify secondary bacterial infection. The officer will also test water quality, especially temperature, dissolved oxygen, ammonia and pH, because poor water is often the real root cause. To help, the farmer should keep a few live affected fish in a bucket of pond water, keep a record of when deaths started, how many fish have died each day, recent handling or stocking, feeding amounts, water source and any changes in weather, and, if possible, take clear photos of the affected fish and eggs.
firstSteps: Remove all dead and dying fish and all dead or mouldy eggs at once, and bury them away from the water or dispose of them as your fisheries officer advises; never throw them back into a pond or stream.
Stop all netting, sorting, grading and transport of the affected fish unless absolutely necessary, because every handling causes new skin damage.
Check water quality: improve aeration or water flow to raise oxygen, stop overfeeding, and remove uneaten feed and excess debris from tanks and ponds.
Where you can, move badly affected fish into a separate tank or hapa (net cage) so they do not shed huge numbers of spores into the main pond.
Reduce feeding to what the fish actually eat within a few minutes, as uneaten feed rots and worsens water quality.
Clean and disinfect nets, buckets, hatchery trays and other equipment, and use separate equipment for affected units.
Record daily deaths, water temperature and what you have observed, and take photos to show the expert.

Contact your County Fisheries Officer, a vet with fish experience or your hatchery supplier for advice before using any salt bath or chemical, as the right product and strength depend on the fish species, size and water.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment focuses on killing or slowing the mould on the fish or eggs and, more importantly, fixing the stress that allowed it to grow. Expert advice is essential, and any chemical treatment should be chosen and prescribed by a vet or qualified fisheries officer. A common first approach for table fish is a salt (sodium chloride) bath or longer exposure to salt in the water, which helps fish keep their body salt balance and discourages mould; the correct strength and time differ greatly between tilapia, catfish and trout, so it must not be guessed. For hatchery eggs and some fish, approved disinfectants such as hydrogen peroxide, and in some places formalin or bronopol-based products, may be used as short baths under strict guidance, since too strong a dose can kill eggs and fish. Malachite green was once widely used but is banned for food fish in many countries because it leaves harmful residues, and it should not be used on fish meant for eating. Antibiotics do not kill water moulds and will not cure Saprolegnia; they are only considered if a vet confirms a bacterial infection alongside the mould, and must be used responsibly to avoid antimicrobial resistance. Where any drug or chemical is used, the vet will give a withdrawal period, a time during which treated fish must not be harvested or sold for food. Fish with mild, early patches often recover once handling stops and water improves, while fish with heavy gill or whole-body infection may not survive and are best removed.
prevention: Handle fish as little and as gently as possible: use soft, knotless nets, wet your hands, keep fish in water during sorting and avoid crowding them in buckets or nets.
Keep good water quality by not overstocking, feeding only what fish eat, maintaining aeration or water flow, and checking oxygen, ammonia and temperature regularly where you can.
Remove dead fish daily and, in hatcheries, remove dead and unfertilised eggs at least once a day using a soft tool or pipette.
In hatcheries, use clean, well-oxygenated water, keep egg trays and jars clean, and ask your hatchery adviser about approved routine egg disinfection.
Plan handling, harvesting, grading and transport for warmer parts of the day and avoid them in the coldest weeks when possible.
Avoid sudden temperature changes by acclimatising new fish slowly and protecting ponds from large inflows of cold rain or borehole water.
Quarantine new fingerlings or broodstock in a separate tank for a period before mixing them with your stock, and buy only from reputable certified hatcheries.
Feed a good-quality, balanced fish feed stored dry and away from heat to keep fish strong, and separate catfish by size to reduce biting.
Control predators such as birds and otters with netting or bird lines, and treat skin parasites early with expert advice so wounds do not form.
Between production cycles, drain, dry and lime ponds where appropriate, and regularly clean and disinfect nets, tanks and equipment.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan fish farm, Saprolegnia can cause serious losses in hatcheries, where whole batches of catfish, tilapia or trout eggs can be lost if dead eggs are not removed, cutting fingerling supply and income. In grow-out ponds and tanks, deaths after handling, transport or stocking reduce the number of fish that reach market size. Sick fish stop feeding and grow slowly, so the farmer spends more on feed for less weight gained. Fish with mould patches, sores and ragged fins look unattractive and may be rejected or fetch lower prices at local markets and hotels. Broodstock losses after spawning are expensive because good breeding fish take time and money to replace. There are also extra costs for treatment, labour and expert visits, and repeated outbreaks can damage a hatchery's reputation with customers.
detail.humanHealth: Saprolegnia water mould is not known to infect people, so normal handling of affected fish carries no direct infection risk; washing hands after handling fish and pond water is still good hygiene. The main human concern comes from the chemicals used to treat fish. Some products, such as formalin and strong hydrogen peroxide, irritate skin, eyes and lungs, so wear gloves and eye protection and use them only in well-ventilated areas as instructed. Fish treated with any chemical must not be harvested or sold before the withdrawal period given by the vet or fisheries officer has passed, and banned products such as malachite green must never be used on food fish because they can leave harmful residues.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early the problem is noticed, how much of the fish is covered and whether the underlying cause is fixed. Fish with small patches on the skin or fins often recover once handling stops, water quality improves and temperatures rise, sometimes with the help of expert-guided salt or disinfectant treatment. Fish with heavy infection of the gills, head or large parts of the body, or with deep sores and bacterial infection, often die even with treatment. Eggs that are already covered in mould cannot be saved, but the rest of the batch can be protected by removing dead eggs quickly. Because the mould is always present in water, outbreaks will return unless handling, water quality and hatchery hygiene are improved.

faqs.q: Is this the same as 'cotton wool disease'?
faqs.a: Farmers often use 'cotton wool disease' for any fluffy white growth on fish, but two different problems can look similar. Saprolegnia is a water mould that forms soft, hairy tufts, usually in cool water and on wounds. Columnaris is a bacterial disease that forms flatter, yellowish-white patches, often in warm water. They are treated differently, so it is worth having a fisheries officer or vet check a sample under a microscope.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell fish that had this mould?
faqs.a: The mould itself is not known to harm people, but badly affected fish look poor and should not be sold. Dead or dying fish should be removed and disposed of properly, not sold. If fish have been treated with any chemical, you must wait for the full withdrawal period advised by the vet or fisheries officer before harvesting or selling them for food.

faqs.q: Can I just add salt to the pond to cure it?
faqs.a: Salt is commonly used to help fish with water mould, but it is not a guaranteed cure and the right amount depends on the fish species, size and whether it is a short bath or a whole pond. Too much salt can kill fish, especially catfish and trout, and salting a large earthen pond can be costly and harmful to plants. Always ask your County Fisheries Officer or a vet for the correct method before using salt, and fix handling and water problems at the same time.

faqs.q: Why does it appear mostly in the cold season?
faqs.a: Saprolegnia grows well in cool water, while fish like tilapia and catfish become sluggish and their immune defences slow down when water is cold. In Kenya this often happens around June to August and in highland counties. Trout farms have cool water all year, so they must be careful all the time. Avoiding handling during the coldest weeks and keeping water clean reduces the risk.

faqs.q: Should I use antibiotics?
faqs.a: No, not on your own. Antibiotics do not kill water moulds, so they will not cure Saprolegnia. A vet may only prescribe an antibiotic if tests show a bacterial infection as well. Using antibiotics without need wastes money, can leave residues in fish meant for food, and helps create resistant bacteria that are harder to treat in future.

faqs.q: Will it spread to my other ponds?
faqs.a: The mould spores are already present in most fresh water, so the disease is mostly triggered by stress and injury. However, dead fish, mouldy eggs and dirty equipment release huge numbers of spores and can increase infection in other units. Removing dead fish and eggs quickly, using separate or disinfected nets and buckets, and not moving sick fish between ponds helps protect the rest of your farm.

saprolegnia.seoDescription: Saprolegnia water mould in fish: spot cotton-wool tufts on tilapia, catfish, trout and eggs, act fast, and prevent it with gentle handling and clean water.

card.headline: Tiny white salt-like spots on fish
card.look: Fish have many small white dots, like grains of salt or sugar, scattered over the skin, fins and gills. They often flash, rub against the pond bottom or tank walls, and gasp near the surface.
card.action: Stop all fish movement, boost aeration and clean water flow, and call a vet or County Fisheries Officer quickly, because untreated white spot can kill many fish within days.

detail.summary: White spot, often called Ich, is a common parasitic disease of freshwater fish caused by a single-celled parasite that burrows into the skin and gills. It shows as small white spots and causes irritation, breathing difficulty and death, especially in young fish. In Kenya it affects tilapia, African catfish, carp and ornamental fish in ponds, tanks, hatcheries and aquariums. It spreads fast in crowded, stressed fish, so early action can save a whole stock.
detail.cause: White spot is caused by Ichthyophthirius multifiliis, a protozoan. That means a tiny single-celled organism, too small to see one by one without a microscope. It is covered in fine hairs called cilia that help it move. The feeding stage, called the trophont, burrows under the outer skin and gill lining and feeds on the fish's cells and body fluids. The fish's body forms a small blister around each parasite, and that is the white spot you see. When mature, the parasite breaks out and drops off. On the pond floor, plants or tank walls it forms a cyst called a tomont. Inside the cyst it divides into hundreds or even thousands of young swimming parasites called theronts. These swim off and must find a fish quickly, usually within a day or two, or they die. Each one burrows into a fish and the cycle starts again. So the number of parasites can multiply very fast. The damage comes from many small wounds in the skin, which upset the fish's control of water and salts and let bacteria and fungi enter. The gills are the most dangerous site. Damaged, swollen gills cannot take in oxygen well, so fish suffocate even when the water has enough oxygen. The speed of the life cycle depends on water temperature. In warm water it may take only a few days. In cool water it can take weeks. This matters for treatment, because only the free-swimming stage can be killed by most treatments. Parasites under the skin and inside cysts are protected.
spread: New fish brought in from another farm, hatchery, market or the wild can carry the parasite in their skin or gills even when they look healthy.
Water from rivers, streams, dams or lakes that hold wild fish can carry free-swimming parasites into ponds and tanks.
Wet nets, buckets, transport bags, boots and other shared equipment can carry parasites and cysts from one pond or farm to another.
Cysts on the pond floor, walls, plants and stones release new waves of parasites, so infection keeps building inside the same pond or tank.
Stress lowers the fish's defences and triggers outbreaks, especially after transport, handling, grading, overcrowding or poor water quality.
Sudden drops or swings in water temperature, common in highland ponds and during the cold months around June to August, often set off outbreaks.
In recirculating and aquaponic systems, water shared between tanks lets the parasite spread to every tank linked to the system.
detail.atRisk: All freshwater fish can get white spot, but fry and fingerlings are hit hardest because their small gills are easily damaged. African catfish (Clarias), which have no scales, and ornamental fish such as goldfish and koi are very sensitive. Nile tilapia and common carp also suffer outbreaks, especially in hatcheries and nursery ponds. Risk is highest in crowded tanks, hatcheries, recirculating systems, aquaponics and small ponds with poor water exchange. Farms in cooler highland areas and fish moved between farms or newly stocked are at special risk. Outbreaks are common after transport, during cool spells and after a sudden change in weather, such as cold nights in the long rains or the cold dry season. Fish that are underfed, kept in dirty water with high ammonia, or recovering from another illness are also more likely to get sick.

early: A few small white spots, about the size of a grain of salt, appear on the fins, tail or body of some fish.
Fish flash, meaning they suddenly turn and rub their sides against the bottom, walls or stones to scratch an itch.
Fish become restless, dart around or hold their fins close to the body.
Some fish eat less and do not rush to the feed as usual.
Fish may gather near the water inlet or the aerator where there is more oxygen.
Gills may be affected before any spots show on the skin, so unusual breathing can be the first sign.
advanced: Many white spots cover the skin, fins and gills, sometimes so many that the fish looks dusted with salt.
Fish gasp at the surface and breathe fast, with gill covers moving quickly, because the gills are damaged.
Gills look pale, swollen or covered in mucus when you gently lift the gill cover.
The skin becomes cloudy with extra slime, and patches of skin may peel, leaving raw-looking areas.
Fish stop eating, become weak, hang still in the water or lie on the bottom.
Secondary bacterial or fungal infections appear, such as red sores or cotton-like growths.
Fish start dying, often many per day, with young fish dying first.

lookalikes.name: Fungal infection (Saprolegnia, water mould)
lookalikes.howToTell: Fungus grows as white or grey fluffy tufts like cotton wool, usually on wounds or damaged areas, not as separate salt-sized dots spread evenly over the body.

lookalikes.name: Columnaris (bacterial cotton-mouth or saddleback)
lookalikes.howToTell: Columnaris causes larger greyish-white or yellowish patches, often on the mouth, fins or as a band across the back, and the patches spread and erode the skin rather than appearing as many tiny raised spots.

lookalikes.name: Other skin and gill parasites (Trichodina, Costia, gill flukes)
lookalikes.howToTell: These also cause flashing, extra slime and gasping, but they do not usually make clear white dots. A vet must look at a skin scrape or gill sample under a microscope to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Low oxygen or poor water quality
lookalikes.howToTell: Fish gasp at the surface, often early in the morning, but have no white spots. Many fish are affected at once, and testing oxygen and ammonia, or adding aeration, quickly shows the problem.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or fish health officer usually confirms white spot by catching a few affected fish and taking a skin scrape and a small gill sample. These are looked at under a microscope straight away. The parasite is large for a protozoan, round, covered in cilia, moves slowly in a rolling way and has a typical horseshoe-shaped nucleus, which makes it fairly easy to identify by someone trained. Fish that have just died can also be checked, but the parasite may leave dead fish within hours, so live, sick fish give the best result. The officer will also check water quality, because poor water often drives the outbreak and affects which treatment is safe. To prepare, keep a few live sick fish in a clean bucket or bag of their own pond water with air, do not freeze them, and do not add any chemicals before the visit. Write down when signs started, how many fish have died each day, recent fish movements or new stock, feeding, water source and any recent changes in weather or water temperature. If you have a test kit, record oxygen, temperature, pH and ammonia. Know the size or volume of your pond or tank, because treatment depends on it.
firstSteps: Stop moving fish in or out of the affected pond or tank, and do not sell, share or restock until a vet or fisheries officer has advised you.
Increase aeration and water flow if you can, because damaged gills need more oxygen, and flushing with clean water carries away some free-swimming parasites.
Reduce feeding to what the fish clear quickly and remove uneaten feed, since rotting feed fouls the water and stresses sick fish further.
Remove dead and dying fish every day, bury them away from water or dispose of them as advised, and never throw them into other ponds or rivers.
Use separate nets, buckets and boots for the affected unit, and clean and dry them after use so you do not carry the parasite to healthy ponds.
Avoid handling, grading or transporting the fish, because stress makes the disease worse.
Do not add salt, copper, formalin, dyes or other chemicals on your own, because the wrong amount can kill fish quickly and some products are banned for food fish.
Record daily deaths, signs and water readings, then call a vet, County Fisheries Officer or aquaculture extension officer as soon as possible.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be chosen and prescribed by a vet or qualified fish health professional, because the right product and strength depend on the fish species, their size, the water volume, water hardness, temperature and whether the fish are for food. Treatments only kill the free-swimming young parasites and the swimming stage leaving the fish. Parasites under the skin and in cysts are protected, so treatment has to be repeated several times over the whole life cycle, and the timing depends on water temperature. Stopping too early is a common reason spots return. Common options include salt (sodium chloride) baths or longer salt treatments, which many fish such as tilapia tolerate well, though some species tolerate it less. Formalin is used in some hatcheries and tanks, but it reduces oxygen in the water and is dangerous to people, so it needs strong aeration and careful handling. Copper sulphate and potassium permanganate are sometimes used, but they are toxic to fish if the dose is wrong, especially in soft water. Malachite green, an old dye treatment, is banned for food fish in many countries because of residue concerns and must not be used on fish for eating. In aquariums, a vet may advise slowly raising the water temperature for species that tolerate it, which speeds up the cycle so treatment works faster; this is rarely practical in ponds. In flow-through tanks and raceways, increased water flow and frequent cleaning of the bottom help remove cysts. Treating a large earthen pond can be costly and difficult, so the vet may advise focusing on aeration, water exchange and partial harvest. If secondary bacterial infections are present, the vet may consider an antibiotic, but antibiotics do not kill the Ich parasite. Use them only when prescribed, to protect against antimicrobial resistance, which is when germs stop responding to medicines. For any chemical or drug used in food fish, follow the withdrawal period, meaning the time you must wait before harvesting and selling fish, as set by the vet and the label. Expect fish to stop dying within days if treatment works, with spots clearing over one to two weeks depending on temperature.
prevention: Buy fingerlings only from certified, reputable hatcheries, and ask about recent disease problems before buying.
Quarantine all new fish in a separate tank or pond for at least two to three weeks, watching for spots, flashing and gasping before mixing them with your stock.
Avoid filling ponds directly from rivers, streams or dams with wild fish where possible; use screened or filtered inlets, boreholes or settled water, and never put wild-caught fish into your ponds.
Keep stocking densities sensible for your system and keep water clean, with good oxygen, by regular partial water changes and avoiding overfeeding.
Reduce temperature shocks by keeping ponds at a good depth, avoiding sudden large additions of cold water, and being extra watchful in cool months and after cold nights.
Handle and transport fish gently and only when needed, using clean water of similar temperature, to limit stress.
Between production cycles, drain, dry and lime earthen ponds, and clean and disinfect tanks, so cysts in the mud and on walls are destroyed.
Give each pond or tank its own nets and buckets, or clean and dry shared equipment fully between units, and limit visitors walking from farm to farm.
Feed a good-quality, fresh, properly stored fish feed in the right amount so fish stay strong and better able to resist infection.
detail.impact: White spot can cause heavy losses on Kenyan fish farms, especially in hatcheries and nursery ponds where fry and fingerlings can die in large numbers within a few days. For a hatchery, an outbreak can wipe out a batch of fingerlings meant for sale to other farmers, causing lost income and damaged reputation. In grow-out ponds and cages, sick fish stop eating and grow slowly, so harvest is delayed and feed, the biggest cost in fish farming, is wasted. Survivors with scarred skin and secondary infections may look poor at market and sell for less. Treatment costs, extra aeration, water pumping and labour add to expenses, and fish movement must stop, delaying sales and restocking. Because the parasite can live on in pond mud and equipment, one outbreak can affect later cycles if ponds are not cleaned well.
detail.humanHealth: White spot does not infect people, and fish that recover are not a disease risk to the people who eat them. The human risk comes from the chemicals used to treat it. Formalin and some other products are harmful to breathe or touch, so wear gloves and protect your eyes and skin when a vet advises their use. Banned chemicals such as malachite green can leave residues in fish meat, so never use them on food fish, and always observe the withdrawal period before harvesting fish treated with any chemical or drug.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when white spot is noticed early, the cause of stress is fixed and the full course of treatment is completed across the whole life cycle. Fish with only a few skin spots usually recover well. The outlook is poorer when the gills are badly damaged, when fry or very young fingerlings are affected, when water quality is poor or when secondary bacterial and fungal infections set in. Outbreaks in cool water last longer because the parasite develops slowly and treatment must continue for longer. Large earthen ponds are harder to treat than tanks. Fish that survive often develop some resistance to reinfection for a time, but this protection is not complete and new fish brought in can start a fresh outbreak.

faqs.q: Can we eat fish that have white spot?
faqs.a: The Ich parasite does not infect people, so properly cooked fish from an affected pond are not a disease danger. However, very sick fish are of poor quality and should not be sold. If the fish have been treated with any chemical or drug, you must wait for the withdrawal period advised by the vet before harvesting, and never sell fish treated with banned products such as malachite green.

faqs.q: Is ordinary salt enough to treat white spot?
faqs.a: Salt is one of the treatments vets use, and many fish, including tilapia, tolerate it well. But the right type of salt, strength and length of treatment depend on the species, the fish size and the exact volume of water. Too little does not work and too much can kill fish, and some species such as catfish may be more sensitive. Get the plan from a vet or fisheries officer rather than guessing, and use plain salt without additives such as iodine or anti-caking agents unless advised otherwise.

faqs.q: I treated once and the spots went away, but now they are back. Why?
faqs.a: Treatments only kill the swimming stage of the parasite. The ones under the skin and inside cysts on the pond floor are protected. When they mature, a new wave of swimming parasites comes out and attacks the fish again. That is why treatment must be repeated over the whole life cycle as your vet advises. Spots disappearing from the fish does not always mean the parasite is gone from the water.

faqs.q: Will white spot go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes a mild outbreak settles if the fish are strong, the water is clean and the temperature becomes warmer. But it can also explode very quickly, because each parasite can produce hundreds of new ones. In fry, fingerlings and crowded ponds, waiting often leads to heavy deaths. It is safer to improve aeration and water quality straight away and get professional advice.

faqs.q: Can white spot spread from one pond to my other ponds?
faqs.a: Yes. The parasite travels in water, on wet nets, buckets and boots, and in fish moved between ponds. Keep separate equipment for the sick pond, clean and dry tools between uses, do not let water from the sick pond flow into others, and do not move fish until the outbreak is over.

faqs.q: How can I stop it coming in with new fingerlings?
faqs.a: Buy from a certified hatchery, check the fish closely on arrival, and keep them in a separate quarantine tank or small pond for at least two to three weeks before mixing them with other fish. Avoid sudden temperature changes when releasing them by slowly mixing pond water into the transport bag. Watch for white spots, flashing and gasping during quarantine and call for advice if you see them.
