white-spot.seoDescription: White spot (Ich) in fish: spot salt-like white dots, flashing and gasping in tilapia and catfish ponds, first steps, vet treatment and prevention in Kenya.

card.headline: Tiny discs or threads stuck on fish
card.look: Flat, see-through, greenish discs that move on the skin (fish lice), or thin white-green threads, often with two tails, sticking out of red spots (anchor worm). Fish flash, jump and rub against the pond sides and bottom.
card.action: Net a few fish, look closely at their skin, fins and gills, and call your County Fisheries Officer or an aquaculture vet before using any chemical in the pond.

detail.summary: Fish lice (Argulus) and anchor worm (Lernaea) are two small crustacean parasites, distant relatives of crabs and shrimps, that attach to the outside of fish. They feed on skin, blood and body fluids, leaving red sores that bacteria and fungus can easily invade. They are common in warm ponds in Kenya, especially where new fish are brought in without checks or river water enters unscreened. Light infestations mostly slow growth, but heavy ones can kill fingerlings and make table and ornamental fish unsellable.
detail.cause: Fish lice (Argulus) are flat, round to oval parasites, usually a few millimetres across and up to about the size of a fingernail. They are almost transparent or greenish, so they blend in with the fish. They hold on with two strong suckers and can swim freely from fish to fish. To feed, a louse pierces the skin with a sharp mouthpart and injects digestive juices, then sucks blood and tissue fluid. This leaves small red pinpoint wounds that become swollen and inflamed. Adult females leave the fish to lay rows of eggs on hard surfaces such as stones, pond walls, sticks and pipes. Anchor worm (Lernaea) is a different parasite. Only the adult female attaches. She buries her head deep into the fish's skin and muscle, and the head grows into an anchor-shaped hook that holds her in place. What the farmer sees is the thin body, about one to two centimetres long, hanging out of the fish, often with two small egg sacs at the end that look like a split tail. Around the entry point the flesh becomes red, swollen and sometimes ulcerated. The young stages of anchor worm swim free in the water and also feed on fish, including on the gills. With both parasites, the real danger is often what follows: the open wounds let in bacteria such as Aeromonas and water moulds (fungus), which cause ulcers, fin rot and deaths. Constant irritation also stresses the fish, so they eat less, grow slowly and become more likely to catch other diseases. Fish lice have also been reported to carry some viral and bacterial diseases from fish to fish.
spread: Bringing in infested fingerlings, brood stock or ornamental fish from another farm, hatchery or market is the most common way both parasites reach a new pond.
Wild fish entering through unscreened inlets from rivers, dams or canals can carry lice and anchor worms into a clean pond.
Free-swimming young parasites and adult fish lice move with the water, so water flowing from one pond to the next can carry them downstream.
Nets, buckets, seine nets and transport containers moved wet between ponds can carry eggs and young parasites.
Fish lice eggs stuck on stones, pond walls, roots and debris can survive after the fish are harvested and hatch when the pond is restocked if it is not dried and cleaned.
Warm water speeds up the life cycle of both parasites, so numbers can build up very quickly during hot, dry spells and in shallow, warm ponds.
Overcrowding, poor water quality, low oxygen and too much organic waste stress the fish and let parasite numbers rise faster.
detail.atRisk: All farmed fish can be affected, but common carp, koi and goldfish are classic hosts, and Nile tilapia and African catfish are also affected in Kenyan ponds. Fingerlings and small fish suffer most because a few parasites take a large share of their small body. Problems are most common in earthen ponds fed by river or canal water, in ponds stocked with fish from unknown sources, and in overstocked ponds with poor water exchange. Warm seasons and warm lowland areas, such as the Lake Victoria basin and coastal regions, favour fast parasite build-up, but ponds in central Kenya can also be hit during hot dry months. Ornamental fish ponds and aquariums that keep adding new fish are at high risk. Cage farms in lakes can be exposed through wild fish living around the cages.

early: Fish flashing, which means suddenly turning on their side so the belly flashes silver in the light.
Fish rubbing or scraping their bodies against the pond walls, bottom, stones or nets.
Fish jumping out of the water more than usual, or darting about restlessly.
Small flat discs that move across the skin or fins when you look closely at a netted fish, or thin threads sticking out of the skin.
Small red pinpoint spots or slightly raised red patches on the skin, often near the fins or base of the tail.
Fish slightly slower to come to feed or eating less than normal.
advanced: Many lice or anchor worms visible on each fish, sometimes in the mouth, on the gills or around the eyes.
Red, swollen, open sores and ulcers around the attachment points, sometimes with white cotton-wool tufts of fungus.
Ragged, frayed or reddened fins and loss of scales.
Thin fish with poor growth and uneven sizes in the same pond.
Fish gasping at the surface or crowding near the water inlet, especially if gills are damaged or oxygen is low.
Daily deaths, often starting with fingerlings and the weakest fish.
Harvested fish with marked, scarred or sore skin that buyers reject or pay less for.

lookalikes.name: White spot disease (Ich)
lookalikes.howToTell: White spot shows as many tiny white dots like grains of salt or sugar scattered over the skin and fins. The dots do not move and do not stick out as threads. Fish lice are larger, flat and move around, and anchor worms are visible threads with a tail.

lookalikes.name: Fish leeches
lookalikes.howToTell: Leeches are longer, worm-like and segmented, with a sucker at each end. They move by looping like an inchworm and stretch and shrink. Fish lice are flat and round, and anchor worms stay fixed in one place with the head buried in the flesh.

lookalikes.name: Bacterial ulcer and fin rot (such as Aeromonas infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Bacterial disease also causes red sores and ragged fins, but when you look closely there are no lice or threads on the fish. Note that the two often go together, because bacteria invade parasite wounds, so a vet may find both.

lookalikes.name: Poor water quality or tiny skin flukes
lookalikes.howToTell: High ammonia, low oxygen or microscopic parasites like flukes also cause flashing and rubbing, but you will not see anything on the skin with the naked eye. A water test and a skin or gill scraping under a microscope are needed to tell them apart.

detail.diagnosis: Fish lice and anchor worms are usually large enough to see with the naked eye, so diagnosis often starts with simply netting several fish and examining them closely in good light, ideally with a magnifying glass. The vet or fisheries officer will check the skin, fins, mouth and gills, count roughly how many parasites each fish has, and may scrape a little mucus from the skin and gills to look under a microscope for young parasite stages and other parasites such as flukes or white spot. They will look for secondary bacterial or fungal infection in the sores, and may send swabs or whole sick fish to a laboratory if deaths are high. Because water quality affects how badly fish suffer, they will usually test or ask about oxygen, temperature, ammonia and pH. To prepare, keep a few live, affected fish in a clean bucket or plastic bag of their own pond water with air, rather than dead or frozen ones. Write down when signs started, the number of deaths per day, the source and date of your last stocking, the stocking density, feed type and amount, water source, and any treatments already used.
firstSteps: Net a few fish from each affected pond and look closely at their skin, fins and gills in good light so you know what you are dealing with and how many fish are affected.
Stop moving fish, water and equipment between ponds, and do not sell or give away live fish from affected ponds, so you do not spread the parasites to clean ponds or other farms.
Remove dead and dying fish every day and dispose of them by burying them away from the pond with lime or burning them, never throwing them into rivers or other ponds.
Check and improve water quality: if you can, increase aeration or add clean, screened water, and remove rotting feed, weeds and debris.
Reduce feeding to what the fish clear quickly, because uneaten feed rots, lowers oxygen and stresses fish further.
Clean and dry nets, buckets and boots after use, and keep a separate set of equipment for the affected pond if possible.
Do not pour livestock dips, crop pesticides or household chemicals into the pond; many are deadly to fish and leave dangerous residues in fish people will eat.
Keep a written record of signs, deaths and dates, then call your County Fisheries Officer, an aquaculture extension officer or a vet who handles fish for advice on safe treatment.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be planned and prescribed by a vet or qualified fisheries health officer, because the wrong chemical or amount can kill all the fish, and some products are not allowed for food fish. Treatment usually targets both the parasites on the fish and the eggs and young stages in the water, so more than one step is often needed over several weeks. For small numbers of valuable fish such as koi or brood stock, anchor worms can be gently pulled out with fine forceps close to the skin, and the wound cleaned, by a trained person. Short salt baths or dips are sometimes used to reduce lice and help the skin heal, but salt does not reliably kill embedded anchor worms. For whole ponds, a vet may recommend approved anti-parasite treatments; drug groups used in aquaculture in different countries include chitin-inhibitors such as diflubenzuron or lufenuron, which stop the parasites from growing their shell, in-feed treatments such as emamectin benzoate, and older organophosphate chemicals, some of which are now restricted or banned for food fish. Products such as potassium permanganate or formalin are sometimes used for skin infections but must be handled with great care. Which products are legal and available in Kenya varies, so rely on your vet. Fish lice eggs stuck to hard surfaces resist most treatments, so after harvest the vet may advise draining, drying and liming the pond to break the cycle. If sores are badly infected with bacteria, a vet may prescribe an antibiotic, usually given in medicated feed. Antibiotics do not kill the parasites themselves, and should only be used when truly needed, because misuse in ponds creates antibiotic-resistant bacteria that harm fish and people. Every drug used in food fish has a withdrawal period, a set number of days during which the fish must not be harvested or eaten. Follow the vet's instructions and the label exactly. Expect fish to start eating better and rubbing less within days to weeks if treatment works, and sores to heal more slowly.
prevention: Buy fingerlings and brood stock only from certified, reputable hatcheries, and ask about their parasite and disease history.
Quarantine all new fish in a separate tank or small pond for at least two to three weeks, checking them closely for lice and threads before adding them to your main ponds.
Screen water inlets with fine mesh or pass river water through a simple sand or gravel filter to keep out wild fish and free-swimming parasites.

Between production cycles, drain the pond fully, let the bottom dry and crack in the sun, remove mud and debris, and apply agricultural lime as advised by your extension officer to kill eggs and larvae.
Keep stocking density within recommended levels for your pond size and species, and maintain good water quality with regular water exchange, aeration where possible and careful feeding.
Check a sample of fish every week or two, especially in hot dry months, so you catch a few parasites before they become thousands.

For fish lice, some farmers place smooth boards or tiles in the pond as egg-laying surfaces, then lift, dry or scrub them regularly to remove the eggs; ask your fisheries officer if this suits your system.
Keep separate nets and buckets for each pond or disinfect and dry them between ponds, and do not let water from an infested pond flow into clean ones.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan fish farm, fish lice and anchor worms mainly cost money through slower growth, poorer feed conversion and losses of fingerlings. Fish that are constantly irritated eat less and turn more of their feed into fighting the parasites than into flesh, so it takes longer and costs more in feed to reach market size. Heavy infestations can kill many fingerlings within weeks, wasting the money spent on stocking. Table tilapia and catfish with red sores, scars and missing scales fetch lower prices or are rejected by hotels, supermarkets and traders, and ornamental koi and goldfish can lose most of their value. Secondary bacterial infections can cause bigger die-offs. Treatment, extra labour for checking fish, pond drying and lost production time between cycles add further costs. Because parasites spread easily, an infested hatchery or farm can damage its reputation with buyers of fingerlings.
detail.humanHealth: Fish lice and anchor worms do not infect people, and properly cleaned and well-cooked fish from a pond with these parasites is not known to be harmful. Cut away and discard any badly ulcerated or infected parts of the flesh and cook fish thoroughly. The main human risk comes from chemical residues: never use livestock dips, crop pesticides or unapproved products in fish ponds, and always observe the withdrawal period of any treatment before harvesting, selling or eating the fish. Wear gloves when handling pond chemicals such as lime, potassium permanganate or formalin, avoid breathing fumes, and wash hands after handling sick fish, as some bacteria in fish sores can infect cuts on human skin.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when infestations are found early and the farmer combines vet-guided treatment with better pond management. Lightly affected fish usually recover, start eating normally again and their small wounds heal over a few weeks, although scars may remain. Fingerlings, heavily infested fish and fish with badly infected sores or damaged gills are less likely to recover. Parasites often come back if only the fish are treated and the eggs and young stages in the pond are ignored, or if new infested fish or unscreened water keep coming in. Breaking the cycle by drying and liming ponds, quarantining new stock and screening inlets gives the best long-term results, but no single step guarantees the pond stays free.

faqs.q: Can I eat fish that had fish lice or anchor worms?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. These parasites do not infect people. Remove the parasites, cut away any badly damaged or ulcerated flesh, and cook the fish well. If the fish were treated with any drug or chemical, do not eat or sell them until the withdrawal period given by your vet or on the label has passed.

faqs.q: Can I just pull the anchor worms out by hand?
faqs.a: For a few valuable fish such as koi or brood fish, a trained person can remove anchor worms with fine forceps, pulling gently close to the skin so the head comes out. If the head breaks off inside it can cause infection, so ask your vet first. Pulling worms off a whole pond of table fish is not practical, and it does not deal with the young parasites in the water.

faqs.q: Will adding salt to my pond get rid of them?
faqs.a: Salt can help fish heal and may reduce some fish lice when used as a short bath for small numbers of fish, but it does not reliably kill embedded anchor worms or eggs on pond surfaces. Salting a whole earthen pond takes very large amounts and can harm some fish and plants. Ask your fisheries officer or vet before using salt, and follow their guidance.

faqs.q: I treated my pond but the parasites came back. Why?
faqs.a: Both parasites have stages that are hard to kill. Fish lice eggs stick to stones and walls and resist most treatments, and anchor worm larvae live in the water. If treatment only kills adults, new parasites hatch a few weeks later. New fish or unscreened river water can also bring them back. Your vet may recommend repeat treatments, and drying and liming the pond after harvest is one of the best ways to break the cycle.

faqs.q: Can I use cattle dip or tick spray in my fish pond?
faqs.a: No. Livestock dips and crop pesticides are made for land animals or plants and are often extremely poisonous to fish, even in tiny amounts. They can wipe out your whole pond, poison downstream water and leave dangerous residues in fish people eat. Only use products a vet has prescribed for fish.

faqs.q: Do tilapia and catfish really get these parasites, or only koi and goldfish?
faqs.a: Carp, koi and goldfish are the best-known hosts, but tilapia and African catfish in Kenyan ponds can also be affected, especially fingerlings and fish in crowded, warm ponds with poor water quality. Checking a sample of your fish regularly is the best way to know whether your pond has a problem.

card.headline: Red blotches and ulcers on fish
card.look: Fish show red patches or bleeding spots on the skin, fins and belly, often with open sores, ragged fins, a swollen belly or bulging eyes. Sick fish stop feeding, hang near the surface or pond edges, and a few die every day.
card.action: Remove dead and dying fish, stop feeding for the day, add fresh water and aeration, and call a vet or County Fisheries Officer quickly.

aka: Ugonjwa wa vidonda vyekundu (red sore disease)
detail.summary: Motile Aeromonas septicaemia (MAS) is a bacterial infection of fish caused mainly by Aeromonas hydrophila and related Aeromonas bacteria. Septicaemia means the bacteria have entered the blood and spread through the body. It is one of the most common causes of red sores and deaths in farmed catfish and tilapia in Kenya and East Africa. It almost always follows stress or poor water quality, so it is as much a warning about pond management as it is a disease.
detail.cause: Aeromonas bacteria live naturally in almost all fresh water, pond mud and even in the gut of healthy fish. Normally a healthy fish with intact skin and slime keeps them out. When fish are stressed by low oxygen, high ammonia (a toxic waste from fish droppings and rotting feed), crowding, rough handling, transport, sudden temperature changes or parasite damage, their immune defences drop and the skin may be scratched. The bacteria then enter through damaged skin, gills or the gut. They release toxins and enzymes that break down blood vessels and tissue. This causes the red blotches (bleeding under the skin), ulcers (open sores where skin and muscle are eaten away), fin rot (fins fraying and dying back) and damage to internal organs such as the kidney, liver and spleen. When the kidney fails, fluid builds up in the body cavity, giving the swollen belly and sometimes raised scales and bulging eyes. In short, the bacteria are opportunists: they take advantage of fish already weakened by poor conditions.
spread: Poor water quality is the main trigger: low dissolved oxygen, high ammonia or nitrite, very green or murky water, and rotting uneaten feed all stress fish and feed the bacteria.
Overstocking, where too many fish share too little water, raises stress, waste and fighting injuries, letting bacteria build up quickly.
Handling, grading, netting, seining and transport damage the protective slime and scales, so outbreaks often start a few days after fingerlings are stocked or fish are moved.
Sudden temperature swings, such as cold rain falling into a warm pond at the start of the long or short rains, or very hot shallow water in the dry season, weaken the fish.
Dead and dying fish left in the pond release huge numbers of bacteria into the water, so infection spreads to the rest of the stock.
Contaminated nets, buckets, boots and transport tanks moved between ponds, and water flowing from an infected pond into another, carry the bacteria between units.
Buying fingerlings from an unknown or poorly managed hatchery can bring in stressed or already infected fish.
Parasites and other infections that damage the skin and gills open the door for Aeromonas to enter.
detail.atRisk: African catfish (Clarias gariepinus, kambare) and Nile tilapia (ngege or perege) are the species most often affected on Kenyan farms, though almost any freshwater fish can get MAS. Fingerlings and juveniles, newly stocked or recently transported fish, and fish that have just been sorted or harvested from are at the highest risk. Earthen ponds with heavy feeding and little water exchange, overstocked liner ponds and tanks, recirculating systems with failing filters, hatcheries, and cages in lakes or dams during poor-water periods are all vulnerable. Risk rises in the hot dry months when water is shallow and oxygen is low, and at the start of the rains when temperature changes and muddy runoff hit the pond. Farms that overfeed, never test water, or leave dead fish in the pond see more outbreaks.

early: Fish eat less or stop coming up for feed, and more feed than usual is left floating or sinking uneaten.
Fish become slow and dull, hang near the surface, the inlet or the pond edges, or swim lazily on their own away from the shoal.
Skin colour turns darker than normal, and the body may lose its shine as the slime layer changes.
Small red spots or streaks appear at the base of the fins, around the mouth, under the jaw or along the belly.
Fins begin to look frayed, ragged or reddened at the edges, and a few scales may be loose or missing on tilapia.
A small number of fish die each day, often the smaller or weaker ones, instead of a sudden mass kill.
advanced: Large red blotches cover the body, and open ulcers appear that may be grey, white or red in the middle with a red ring around them.
Fins rot back towards the body, and the tail may be badly eroded.
The belly becomes swollen and soft with fluid, and the vent (the opening under the tail) looks red and swollen.
Eyes may bulge outwards (pop-eye) or look cloudy or bloody, and scales may stand out from the body like a pine cone.
Gills may look pale or blotchy instead of a healthy bright red.
Fish swim abnormally, lie on their sides or roll, and daily deaths increase; a cut fish may show bloody fluid in the belly and a swollen, soft kidney or spleen.

lookalikes.name: Columnaris disease (Flavobacterium columnare)
lookalikes.howToTell: Columnaris usually gives greyish-white or yellowish patches, often a pale 'saddle' band behind the head or fuzzy, eaten-looking gills, rather than deep red blotches. It often appears in warm water after handling. Both can occur together, so a lab test is the only sure way to separate them.

lookalikes.name: Streptococcosis in tilapia
lookalikes.howToTell: Streptococcus infection in tilapia typically causes bulging, cloudy eyes, fish spinning or swimming in circles, and a curved body, often in warm water and larger fish. Red skin patches can appear in both, so bacterial culture by a lab is needed to confirm.

lookalikes.name: Epizootic ulcerative syndrome (EUS)
lookalikes.howToTell: EUS is caused by a water mould (Aphanomyces invadans) and produces very deep, crater-like red ulcers that can expose muscle, often after cool weather. It is a WOAH-listed disease, so if a vet suspects it they must investigate and may need to report it. Only lab examination of tissue can tell it apart from MAS.

lookalikes.name: Low oxygen or ammonia poisoning
lookalikes.howToTell: Oxygen crashes usually kill many fish suddenly, often at dawn, with fish gasping at the surface, and the dead fish have no red sores or ulcers. Ammonia stress can cause reddened gills and fins but is confirmed by a water test. Poor water often comes first and MAS follows a few days later.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or trained fish health officer starts by looking at the whole pond: how the fish behave, how many are dying, feeding records, stocking density and recent handling or weather changes. They will test the water for temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, ammonia and nitrite, because finding and fixing the stress is part of the diagnosis. They then examine sick fish closely, checking skin, fins, eyes, gills and the inside of the body during a post-mortem (opening the fish to look at the organs). To confirm Aeromonas, samples from the kidney, liver or ulcers are sent to a laboratory for bacterial culture, and sometimes molecular tests such as PCR. A sensitivity test shows which antibiotics, if any, will actually work against the bacteria on your farm. In Kenya, samples may go to the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, KMFRI (Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute) centres such as Sagana, county or university labs. The best samples are live, sick fish carried in a bag with pond water and air, or fish that have only just died, kept cool on ice but not frozen. Rotten fish are of little use. Before the visit, write down when the problem started, daily deaths, feeding amounts, stocking date and numbers, where the fingerlings came from, any recent handling, and any water test results you have.
firstSteps: Remove dead and dying fish from the pond at least twice a day, and bury them deeply with lime away from water sources or burn them; never throw them into another pond or a river, and never feed them to other animals.
Reduce or stop feeding for a day or two, because sick fish eat little and uneaten feed rots, lowers oxygen and feeds the bacteria; then restart with small amounts the fish actually finish.
Improve the water straight away by adding clean fresh water from a safe source, running aerators or paddle wheels, or splashing water to add oxygen, especially at night and early morning.
Stop all handling, sorting, seining, harvesting and moving of fish from the affected pond, and do not stock new fish until the problem is resolved.
Keep separate nets, buckets and boots for the sick pond, and clean and dry equipment in the sun after use so you do not carry the bacteria to other ponds.
Wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish, avoid touching them with cuts on your hands, and wash your hands well with soap afterwards.
Write down daily deaths, the signs you see, feeding and any water test readings, and keep a few freshly sick fish cool for testing.
Call a vet, the County Fisheries Officer or your aquaculture extension officer early, and do not add antibiotics, chemicals or home remedies to the pond without their advice.
detail.vetTreatment: The first and most important treatment is fixing the cause: the vet will help you correct oxygen, ammonia, stocking density, feeding and water exchange, because drugs will not work if the fish stay stressed. Some fish professionals may advise short supportive measures such as salt treatments or other bath treatments to help the skin and slime recover; these must be done exactly as advised, because wrong strengths can kill fish. When antibiotics are needed, they are usually given in medicated feed, using drugs such as oxytetracycline or florfenicol, but only where a product is registered for fish and prescribed by a vet, ideally after a sensitivity test shows it will work. The vet decides the drug, the amount and how long to feed it. Medicated feed only reaches fish that are still eating, so it helps most when started early; badly sick fish that have stopped feeding often cannot be saved. Antibiotics should never be poured into pond water routinely, as this wastes drugs, harms the pond environment and breeds resistant bacteria. Aeromonas is known for developing antimicrobial resistance, which means the bacteria learn to survive drugs and future outbreaks become harder to treat, so antibiotics must be used responsibly and only under prescription. Any fish treated with antibiotics must not be harvested or sold until the withdrawal period on the product label or given by the vet has passed, so that no drug residues reach consumers. Vaccines against Aeromonas exist in some countries but are not widely available on Kenyan farms. Expect deaths to continue for a few days after treatment begins before they slow down.
prevention: Test water regularly for dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite, pH and temperature using a simple test kit, and act early when readings worsen rather than waiting for fish to die.
Stock at a density your pond, water supply and aeration can support, and harvest or split fish as they grow instead of letting the pond become crowded.
Feed good-quality fish feed at the right amount for fish size and water temperature, feed only what is eaten within a few minutes, and store feed dry and away from mould.
Buy fingerlings from a certified, well-run hatchery, check them for sores and weak swimming before accepting them, and acclimatise them slowly to your pond water temperature.
Handle fish as little and as gently as possible, use smooth knotless nets, avoid handling during the hottest part of the day, and plan grading or transport for cool mornings.
Prepare ponds well between cycles by draining, removing excess mud, sun-drying and liming the bottom, and keep pond banks and inlets clean so runoff does not carry dirt in during the rains.
Remove dead fish every day, keep separate equipment for each pond or clean and dry it between uses, and use a footbath or clean boots when moving between units.

Control predators and birds with netting where possible, manage parasites with advice from a fisheries officer, and keep simple farm records of feeding, deaths and water tests so problems are spotted early.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan fish farm, MAS can cause steady daily losses that add up to a large part of the stock, especially among fingerlings and newly stocked fish. Survivors often grow more slowly because they eat less while sick, which delays harvest and wastes feed, the biggest running cost in fish farming. Fish with red sores and ulcers are hard to sell, as buyers in local markets, hotels and supermarkets reject damaged fish, and a farm's reputation can suffer. Treatment adds costs for testing, medicated feed and extra aeration or water pumping, and fish under antibiotic withdrawal cannot be sold on time. For smallholders who have invested savings or group funds in a pond or cage, one bad outbreak can wipe out a season's profit, so prevention through good water and stocking management pays back many times.
detail.humanHealth: Aeromonas bacteria can occasionally infect people. They can cause wound infections if bacteria from fish or pond water enter cuts or scratches, and stomach upsets with diarrhoea if contaminated fish or water are swallowed. People with weak immune systems, liver disease, diabetes, young children and the elderly are more at risk of serious illness. Wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish, cover any cuts, wash hands and tools well with soap, and seek medical care if a wound becomes red, swollen or painful after working with fish. Do not eat or sell visibly sick, ulcerated or dead fish, and always cook fish thoroughly. If fish have been given antibiotics, do not eat or sell them until the full withdrawal period has passed, because drug residues can harm consumers and add to antibiotic resistance in people.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for the pond as a whole if the problem is caught early and water quality and stress are quickly corrected; deaths usually slow down within days once conditions improve. Fish with only small red spots or mild fin damage often recover and heal if kept in good water. Fish with deep ulcers, a swollen fluid-filled belly, bulging eyes or that have stopped eating rarely recover and are best removed. Losses are higher in fingerlings, in warm, crowded or dirty ponds, and where treatment is delayed or the wrong antibiotic is used. Because the bacteria stay in the water and mud, outbreaks can return whenever fish are stressed again, so long-term success depends on management, not just treatment.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat fish from a pond that has red sore disease?
faqs.a: Do not eat or sell fish that are visibly sick, ulcerated, swollen or already dead. Healthy-looking fish from the same pond that have not been given antibiotics are generally safe if handled hygienically and cooked thoroughly, but ask your vet or fisheries officer first. If the pond has been treated with antibiotics, no fish can be eaten or sold until the withdrawal period is complete.

faqs.q: Can I just buy antibiotics at the agrovet and put them in the pond water?
faqs.a: No. Pouring antibiotics into pond water wastes the drug, harms the useful bacteria and algae in the pond, leaves residues in fish and breeds bacteria that resist treatment. Many cases improve with water management alone. If antibiotics are truly needed, a vet should choose a registered product, usually in feed, ideally after a lab sensitivity test, and tell you the withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Why does this disease often appear after I stock new fingerlings?
faqs.a: Catching, packing and transporting fingerlings damages their skin and slime and stresses them badly. Temperature and water differences between the hatchery and your pond add more stress. Aeromonas already in your water then takes its chance, so deaths often begin a few days to two weeks after stocking. Buy from good hatcheries, transport fish in cool hours, and acclimatise them slowly by floating the bags and mixing in pond water gradually.

faqs.q: Should I drain the pond and start again?
faqs.a: Not always. Many outbreaks can be controlled by removing dead fish, improving water and reducing feeding. If losses are very heavy, or the problem keeps returning, your fisheries officer may advise harvesting what can be saved, draining, removing sludge, sun-drying and liming the pond before restocking. Make this decision with professional advice, and never release pond water carrying sick fish into rivers or other ponds.

faqs.q: Why do I see more red sores at the start of the rains?
faqs.a: The first heavy rains can cool a warm pond suddenly, wash mud, manure and soil into the water, and change the pH and oxygen levels. Fish become stressed and their immunity drops, while the extra organic matter feeds bacteria. Protect ponds with diversion trenches and grass on the banks, keep good aeration, and watch fish closely in the days after heavy rain.

faqs.q: Will the disease keep coming back?
faqs.a: Aeromonas lives naturally in water and mud, so you cannot remove it completely. It causes disease mainly when fish are stressed. If you keep stocking density reasonable, test water, feed correctly, handle fish gently and remove dead fish daily, outbreaks become much less frequent and less severe. Repeated outbreaks are a sign that something in the system, such as oxygen, crowding or feeding, needs fixing.
